# AcquisitionOS - Senior Java Backend Developer Interview Preparation Guide

> **IMPORTANT - READ THIS FIRST**
>
> The questions inside this guide are **SAMPLE reference questions** compiled as a framework for the LLM. They are intentionally curated to act as a *base reference*, not an exhaustive list. The interview prep must be expanded to cover **maximum possible questions per category** - easy, medium, hard, and twisted variants - including end-to-end annotation usage, code snippets (Java), runtime logic walk-throughs, ASCII architecture diagrams (application flow, business flow, service flow, data flow, deployment flow), database schema designs, and cloud/deployment/testing scenarios. If any answer feels thin, treat it as a *seed* and expand it with deeper examples, edge cases, and follow-up branches the way a tough interviewer at Uber / Amazon / Meta / NetApp would drill down. The interviewer at these companies will frequently ask for **the logic of an API end-to-end** ("walk me through what happens from Controller → Service → Repository → DB when I call `POST /api/leads`"), so every API question should be answerable with a step-by-step trace including annotations, transaction boundaries, exceptions, and side effects.

**Target audience:** Senior Java Backend Engineer, 3.5 years experience, interviewing for 4+ year capability roles at **Uber (next week), NetApp, and Meta (this month)**.

**Backend story (mandatory framing):** AcquisitionOS backend is presented as a **Java 17 + Spring Boot 3.2.x monolithic layered application** using **Spring Web MVC + Spring Data JPA + Hibernate 6 + PostgreSQL 15 + Redis 7**. The frontend (React 18 + TypeScript 5) is out of scope for backend answers - never mention the actual Next.js backend implementation.

## Quick Reference - Project Summary Card

**Project Name:** AcquisitionOS
**Tagline:** B2B SaaS for AI-powered client acquisition - discover, engage, convert, and manage leads at scale.
**Domain:** B2B Sales / Lead Generation / CRM / Outreach Automation
**Type:** Multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform
**Your Role:** Senior Backend Engineer (individual contributor - backend-heavy, full-stack awareness)
**Experience:** 3.5 years (positioned as 4+ years capable)
**Team Size:** 6 engineers (2 backend, 2 frontend, 1 QA, 1 PM), you owned 70% of backend modules
**Duration:** ~9 months design → MVP → production → 3 minor releases
**Production Status:** Live - serving ~3,200 paying organizations, ~50,000 active users, ~2.1M leads processed cumulatively, 99.94% monthly uptime SLA
**Stack (Backend):** Java 17 LTS, Spring Boot 3.2.x, Spring Web MVC, Spring Data JPA, Hibernate 6, Spring Security 6, Spring Batch, Spring AOP, PostgreSQL 15, Redis 7, HikariCP, Flyway, Kafka (events), Resilience4j, MapStruct, Lombok, JUnit 5, Mockito, Spring Boot Test, Testcontainers, WireMock
**Stack (Frontend):** React 18, TypeScript 5, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TanStack Query, Zustand, shadcn/ui
**Stack (Infra/Cloud):** Docker, AWS EC2 + ECS Fargate, RDS PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ), ElastiCache Redis, S3, CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, GitHub Actions CI/CD, Prometheus + Grafana + Loki, Sentry, OpenTelemetry
**External Integrations:** Stripe (payments + webhooks), Google OAuth2, Gmail SMTP, Google Calendar API, Twilio (WhatsApp), Telegram Bot API, OpenAI/Gemini (AI outreach)

**Elevator Pitch (30 seconds):**
> "AcquisitionOS is a B2B SaaS platform that helps small and mid-size sales teams replace 5–6 disconnected tools - lead scrapers, email outreach tools, CRM, calendar, pipeline manager - with one AI-powered system. On the backend I built a Java 17 / Spring Boot 3.2 monolith layered as Controller-Service-Repository, backed by PostgreSQL 15 and Redis 7. The system discovers leads from public sources, scores them with an AI engine, generates personalised outreach emails, sends them via Gmail or Twilio, books meetings through Google Calendar, and tracks deals through a Kanban-style pipeline. We're at 3,200 paying orgs, ~50K users, 2.1M leads processed, and a 99.94% monthly SLA. I own roughly 70% of the backend including auth (OTP, magic link, Google OAuth), payments (Stripe), the credit/usage metering system, and the AI outreach pipeline."

**Two-Minute Walkthrough Script:**

> "Let me walk you through AcquisitionOS end-to-end.
>
> **Problem:** Small sales teams waste 60% of their day switching between a lead scraper, an email tool, a CRM, a calendar, and a pipeline board. There's no single source of truth, no AI-driven prioritisation, and no closed loop between outreach and revenue.
>
> **Solution:** AcquisitionOS unifies the whole funnel. The user uploads a niche - say 'dentists in Mumbai' - and our **Lead Discovery Pipeline** (Spring Batch job + scraping workers + Google Places / LinkedIn enrichment) returns enriched leads with email, phone, social, revenue estimate, and a 0–100 quality score from our **AI Scoring Engine** (calls Gemini/OpenAI through a Resilience4j-circuit-broken `OutreachService`).
>
> The user picks leads and clicks **Generate Outreach**. Our `OutreachGeneratorService` calls the LLM with a templated prompt + the lead context, returns 3 email variants, deducts **credits** (the platform's internal metered currency - every paid action costs credits; each plan ships a monthly allowance), and stores the generated email in a `messages` table. The user can then send via Gmail SMTP (OAuth'd per-user) or Twilio WhatsApp, with **open/click tracking** via pixel + redirect endpoints. Replies are pulled back via Gmail PubSub or webhook and routed through a **Reply Intelligence** module that classifies intent (interested / not-now / unsubscribe) and moves the lead stage automatically in the **Pipeline**.
>
> When the lead says 'yes', **Meeting Scheduling** kicks in - we use Google Calendar API to read free/busy slots, propose 3 timings, and on confirmation push a calendar invite. A **Spring `@Scheduled` reminder job** fires 24h / 1h before.
>
> Throughout, every paid feature deducts credits atomically (`@Transactional` + pessimistic lock on the `credit_balance` row), every security event is audit-logged via Spring AOP, and every long-running job (lead scraping, sequence execution, reply polling, renewal) runs through a **Spring Batch / `@Async` TaskExecutor** backed by a `job_state` table so we can resume on crash.
>
> **Architecture** is a monolith, deliberately - at 3,200 tenants and ~50K users we are nowhere near the scale where microservices pay for themselves. We chose clean layered separation, bounded contexts inside one codebase (`com.acquisitionos.leads`, `.outreach`, `.meetings`, `.billing`, `.auth`, `.ai`), and a `DomainEventPublisher` (Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`) for in-process decoupling. We've designed the seams so we *can* extract `outreach` or `ai` into separate services when traffic justifies it.
>
> **Scale numbers:** 3,200 paying orgs, ~50K active users, 2.1M leads processed, ~28K outreach emails/day, p95 API latency 180ms, p99 540ms, 99.94% monthly uptime, single Postgres primary + 2 read replicas, Redis cluster (3 shards) for sessions + rate-limits + cache.

## Tech Stack - Authoritative Reference Table

| Layer | Technology | Version | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language | Java | 17 LTS | Records, sealed classes, pattern matching, virtual threads preview, mature GC (G1/ZGC), strong tooling |
| Framework | Spring Boot | 3.2.x | Java 17 baseline, Spring 6, Observability Micrometer, native support (GraalVM), mature starter ecosystem |
| Web | Spring Web MVC | 6.1 | Servlet stack, threaded model (1 thread per request), proven for CRUD-heavy monoliths |
| Persistence | Spring Data JPA | 3.2 | Repository abstraction, query derivation, Pageable, Specifications |
| ORM | Hibernate | 6.4 (Spring Boot 3.2 default) | JPA 3.1, batch fetching, second-level cache hooks, multitenancy filters |
| Security | Spring Security | 6.2 | SecurityFilterChain, MethodSecurity, OAuth2 Login, JwtAuthenticationProvider, OAuth2 Resource Server |
| Database | PostgreSQL | 15 | JSONB columns for tags/settings, CTE + window functions for analytics, GIN indexes for full-text, mature replication |
| Cache / Locks / Rate-limit | Redis | 7 (cluster mode 3 shards) | String/Hash/Sorted Set/ZSet for rate-limit sliding window, SET NX for distributed lock, PubSub for cache invalidation |
| Connection pool | HikariCP | 5.x (Spring Boot default) | Fastest JDBC pool, robust leak detection |
| Migrations | Flyway | 9.x | Versioned SQL scripts, repeatable scripts, baseline + repair, lives next to source |
| Background jobs | Spring Batch + `@Async` + `@Scheduled` | 5.x | Lead discovery (chunk-oriented), email sequences (step-oriented), renewals (cron), reminder polling (fixed-delay) |
| Messaging | Apache Kafka | 3.6 | Audit events, reply intelligence triggers, cross-context pub-sub (in-process we use Spring Events, Kafka for the few extracted services we plan) |
| HTTP client | Spring `WebClient` (Reactor Netty) | 6.1 | Non-blocking, retry, circuit-breaker integration, used for Stripe/Google/Twilio/LLM calls |
| Resilience | Resilience4j | 2.x | Circuit breaker, retry, rate limiter, bulkhead, time-limiter - used around every external call |
| Object mapping | MapStruct | 1.5 | Compile-time DTO ↔ Entity mapping, no runtime reflection |
| Boilerplate | Lombok | 1.18 | `@Data`, `@Slf4j`, `@Builder` - controlled, never on entities (breaks JPA equals/hashCode) |
| Testing | JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring Boot Test, Testcontainers, WireMock | latest | Unit (Mockito), slice (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`), integration (Testcontainers PG + Redis), contract (WireMock for Stripe/Google) |
| API docs | springdoc-openapi | 2.3 (OpenAPI 3) | Auto-generated Swagger UI + ReDoc, contract-first design |
| Monitoring | Micrometer + Prometheus + Grafana | 1.12 | JDK 17 GC/JVM/HTTP/Hikari metrics, custom business meters (credits spent, leads discovered) |
| Logging | SLF4J + Logback (JSON encoder) + Loki | 1.4 | Structured logs, correlation via MDC, trace propagation from OTel |
| Tracing | OpenTelemetry + Tempo / Jaeger | 1.32 | Distributed traces across Controller→Service→DB→External |
| Errors | Sentry | latest | Server-side + frontend error tracking |
| Build | Maven | 3.9 | Multi-module (`common`, `domain`, `app`), Maven profiles per env |
| Container | Docker (Eclipse Temurin JRE 17-jammy) | 24 | Layered jar, distroless ready |
| Orchestrator | AWS ECS Fargate + ALB | latest | 4 task replicas, 2 vCPU / 4 GiB each, autoscaling on CPU + ALB request count |
| Database hosting | Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 15 (Multi-AZ, 2 read replicas) | - | Automated backups, point-in-time recovery, RPO 5 min, RTO 30 min |
| Cache hosting | Amazon ElastiCache for Redis 7 (cluster mode, 3 shards, 1 replica each) | - | Multi-AZ, automatic failover |
| Object storage | Amazon S3 + CloudFront CDN | - | User avatars, uploaded attachments, generated invoices (signed URLs) |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions | - | Build → unit + integration tests → SonarQube → Docker build → push ECR → deploy ECS via blue/green |
| Secrets | AWS Secrets Manager + Spring Cloud AWS | - | DB creds, Stripe keys, Google OAuth secret, JWT signing keys - rotated every 90 days |

### 2. Layered Request Flow - `POST /api/leads/discover` (End-to-End Trace)

```
Client → ALB → ECS task → Spring Security Filter Chain
         │
         ▼
  OncePerRequestFilter (JwtAuthenticationFilter)
     └─ verifies JWT (HS256) using JwtDecoder
     └─ sets SecurityContext.authentication = Authentication(user, authorities)
         │
         ▼
  DispatcherServlet → LeadController.discoverLeads(@Valid DiscoverDto)
         │   @PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('USER','ADMIN')")
         │   @RateLimitAspect key=user.id+ip, limit=20/min  (Redis sliding window)
         │   → 429 if exceeded
         │
         ▼
  LeadService.discoverLeads(DiscoverDto, Principal)
     │   @Transactional(isolation=REPEATABLE_READ)
     │   1. checkPlanEntitlement(user.id, "lead_discovery", dto.maxResults)
     │       └─ CreditService.peek(userId) → throws PlanEntitlementException if no credits
     │   2. idempotency check: DiscoverJobRepository.findByRequestId(dto.requestId)
     │       └─ returns existing job state if present (idempotent retry)
     │   3. create DiscoverJob entity (status=PENDING), persist
     │   4. deduct credits: CreditService.deduct(userId, LEAD_DISCOVERY_COST * maxResults, "discover")
     │       └─ UPDATE credit_balance SET balance = balance - cost WHERE user_id=? AND balance>=cost
     │       └─ throws InsufficientCreditsException if 0 rows affected
     │   5. publish LeadDiscoveryRequestedEvent (Spring ApplicationEventPublisher)
     │   6. return DiscoverJobResponse(jobId)
         │
         ▼
  Async path (separate thread via Spring Batch / TaskExecutor):
     DiscoveryJobRunner.run(jobId)
       ├─ LeadDiscoveryService.discover(niche, location, maxResults)
       │     ├─ Google Places API (WebClient + CircuitBreaker)
       │     ├─ LinkedIn enrichment (WebClient)
       │     └─ for each candidate: LeadEnrichmentService.enrich()
       │           ├─ website screenshot (S3 presigned → external worker)
       │           └─ AI score: AiService.scoreLead(lead) → Gemini API
       ├─ Spring Batch chunk commit every 50 leads (Repository.saveAll)
       ├─ on success: DiscoverJob.status=COMPLETED, publish LeadsDiscoveredEvent
       │     └─ AuditAspect logs event, NotificationService pushes to user
       └─ on failure: DiscoverJob.status=FAILED + retry with backoff (Resilience4j)
```

### 3. Business Flow - Lead → Outreach → Meeting → Deal (Vertical Slice)

```
   [User opens "Discover" tab]
            │
            ▼
   POST /api/leads/discover ───► DiscoverJob (PENDING)
            │                          │ @Async
            ▼                          ▼
   UI polls /api/leads/discover/status/{jobId}   DiscoveryJobRunner scrapes + enriches + scores
            │
            ▼ (COMPLETED + N leads)
   GET /api/leads?filter=stage=discovered  →  list returned
            │
            ▼ (User picks 5)
   POST /api/outreach/generate ─► OutreachService.generate()
            │                       ├─ validates plan + credits
            │                       ├─ AiService.generateEmails(lead context, prompt template)
            │                       ├─ deduct credits (outreach_message × count)
            │                       └─ persist `outreach_message` rows (status=DRAFT)
            ▼
   User reviews email in UI → clicks "Send"
   POST /api/outreach/send
            ├─ OutreachService.send(messageIds)
            ├─ MessageDeliveryService.deliver (channel=GMAIL | WHATSAPP | TELEGRAM)
            │     ├─ Gmail: JavaMailSender via Google OAuth'd token (per-user refresh)
            │     ├─ WhatsApp: Twilio REST API (WebClient + Resilience4j)
            │     └─ Telegram: Telegram Bot API
            ├─ EmailTrackingService.attach(messageId) → pixel URL + click redirect URL
            └─ message.status = SENT, sentAt=now
            ▼
   [Time passes - recipient opens email]
   GET /api/email/open/{trackingId}.png  (1x1 transparent GIF)
            ├─ no auth (public - referer/IP hashed)
            ├─ message.openedAt = now, opens++
            └─ if first open: NotificationService → user, ReplyIntelligence kicked
            ▼
   [Recipient replies]
   Gmail PubSub webhook → /api/webhooks/gmail/reply
            ├─ ReplyIntelligenceService.classify(replyText)
            │     └─ AiService.classifyIntent (interested / not-now / unsubscribe)
            ├─ Lead.stage = REPLIED (or REJECTED if unsubscribe)
            ├─ NotificationService.notify(user, "Lead X replied - interested")
            └─ Reply saved to `lead_communications` table
            ▼
   [User responds → asks for a meeting]
   POST /api/meetings/suggest  ──► MeetingService.suggestSlots(leadId)
            ├─ GoogleCalendarService.listFreeBusy(user.googleCalendarId, range)
            │     └─ Calendar API (WebClient + OAuth2 refresh token)
            ├─ AI picks 3 optimal slots (MeetingIntelligenceService)
            └─ persist `meeting_suggestion` rows
            ▼
   [Lead accepts a slot]
   POST /api/meetings/confirm
            ├─ GoogleCalendarService.createEvent(...)
            ├─ Send calendar invite to both parties
            ├─ Schedule @Scheduled reminder job (24h + 1h before)
            └─ Lead.stage = MEETING_BOOKED
            ▼
   [Meeting happens - call notes added]
   POST /api/meetings/{id}/complete
            ├─ MeetingAssistantService.extractActions(transcript)
            ├─ create `follow_up_action` rows
            └─ Lead.stage = NEGOTIATION →  eventually WON / LOST
            ▼
   [Deal won → billing]
   Deal created → DealService.close(wonDeal)
            ├─ publish DealWonEvent → NotificationService → user
            └─ audit log
```

### 6. Service Communication Patterns

```
  In-process (default)              Cross-service-ready (planned extraction)
  ──────────────────────             ───────────────────────────────────────
  ApplicationEventPublisher ──►      → Kafka topic (audit-events,
  (Spring Events)                       outreach-events, reply-events)
        │                                    │
        ▼                                    ▼
  @TransactionalEventListener        @KafkaListener
  (AFTER_COMMIT)                     (consumers in same JVM today, ready
        │                              to extract when justified)
        ▼
  AuditAspect / NotificationService  AuditConsumer / NotificationConsumer
  / ReplyIntelligenceService         / ReplyIntelligenceConsumer

  Why this hybrid: monolith for now, but the seam is "Kafka topic" so we
  can lift `outreach` or `ai` into its own Spring Boot service with zero
  contract change - just swap in-process listener for Kafka listener.
```

## How To Use This Document

- For each question, **speak the answer aloud** before reading the printed answer - then compare and refine.
- The **KEY TERMS TO MENTION** bullets are anchor words the interviewer is listening for; if you hit 4+ of them, you are signalling depth.
- **FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS** are the natural drill-down an Uber/Meta interviewer will ask - read them *before* your initial answer so you don't burn your follow-up material in the opening answer.
- **RED FLAGS TO AVOID** are interview-killers - any of them marks you as shallow.
- Code snippets are **Java + Spring Boot** syntax only. Never mention JavaScript backend, Node, npm, Prisma, Next.js API routes, or any non-Java backend framework.
- When a diagram says "(for 100k users)" - be ready to re-design for that scale on the whiteboard.

## Interview Difficulty Blueprint — How Hard Should You Prepare?

> **Difficulty mix recommendation for a 4-year engineer at product companies** (based on the Uber / Meta / NetApp / Google / Amazon interview pattern for backend roles):

| Difficulty | Share of questions you should master | What they test | Examples in this guide |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Easy** | ~15–20% | Definitions, annotation syntax, "did you actually use this" | Q3-14 CORS, Q5-18 audit fields, Q7-9 @Cacheable |
| **Medium** | ~40–45% | Feature design, standard patterns, trade-off awareness | Q3-9 @Async, Q5-10 pagination, Q8-4 error format |
| **Hard** | ~25–30% | Internals, concurrency, failure modes, measured numbers | Q5-15 locking, Q6-6 zero-downtime migrations, Q7-5 distributed locks |
| **Twisted / Scenario** | ~10–15% | Debugging live incidents, "what breaks at 10× scale", adversarial follow-up chains | Q2-15 duplicate emails, Q6-15 500M rows, Q7-10 Redis down at peak |

**How interviewers at each target company actually drill:**

- **Uber (your next interview)** — system-design-heavy, real-time and marketplace-shaped thinking. Expect: "walk me through the API end-to-end" (Q2-11, Appendix B), queueing vs inline trade-offs, idempotency under retries, and at-least-once semantics. Uber interviewers love the phrase "what breaks first at 10×?" — rehearse Q2-14, Q6-15, Q12-3. Coding rounds: clean HashMap/stream usage, concurrency (ThreadPoolExecutor sizing is a favorite).
- **NetApp** — deeper JVM and OS-layer probes: GC internals (Q12-9), memory model, file I/O, storage-shaped questions (their domain: expect "how would you design for sequential write throughput"). Hibernate session internals and locking (Q5-9, Q5-15) land well here.
- **Meta** — scale + product thinking combined. "Design for 100M users" variants (Q2-14), move-fast trade-offs (what would you NOT build — Q14-10), and behavioral rounds that drill ownership (Q14-3, Q14-9). They probe metric intuition: know your numbers cold (p95, error budgets, hit rates).
- **Google** — algorithm-adjacent system design, "estimate then design" (the general PDF's Part 5), and API design purity (Q8-4, Q8-10's compatibility machinery impresses here).
- **Amazon** — Leadership Principles woven into technical answers: every STAR story (Category 14) should name the principle it demonstrates (Dive Deep for Q12-5, Ownership for Q14-3, Earn Trust for Q14-3's credit-grant, Deliver Results for Q14-4).

**The twisted-question ladder** — how interviewers escalate one topic (practice climbing it aloud):

1. "How does your credit deduction work?" → (normal)
2. "Two requests deduct simultaneously — exactly what happens at the row level?" → (hard)
3. "Now the DB is a read replica behind by 2 seconds — what does the user see?" → (twisted)
4. "You can't change the schema. Fix it in code." → (expert-twisted)

Every question in this guide lists its follow-up chain — practice answering level 2-4 BEFORE the interview, because that's where offers are decided.

# Category 1 & 2 — Project Introduction + System Design

> **SAMPLE QUESTIONS NOTICE:** The questions below are sample reference questions. Treat this as a base framework — the candidate should expand each into deeper follow-ups, twisted variants, and edge cases the way an Uber/Meta interviewer would drill down.

---

## CATEGORY 1 — PROJECT INTRODUCTION QUESTIONS

### Q1-1: Tell me about your most impactful project
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
The most impactful project I've worked on is AcquisitionOS — a B2B SaaS platform I've been building for the last ~9 months as the senior backend engineer. It replaces the disconnected stack of tools that small and mid-size sales teams use today (lead scraper, email tool, CRM, calendar, pipeline manager) with one AI-powered system that handles the entire funnel from "find a lead" to "close a deal".

My contribution on the backend was roughly 70% of the codebase — Java 17 with Spring Boot 3.2 as the framework, PostgreSQL 15 as the primary store, Redis 7 for caching and rate-limiting, and a handful of external integrations (Stripe, Google OAuth + Calendar + Gmail PubSub, Twilio WhatsApp, Telegram bots, OpenAI/Gemini for the AI outreach). The backend is a deliberately-monolithic layered architecture — Controller → Service → Repository → DB — because at our scale (3,200 paying orgs, ~50K users) microservices would pay for themselves only at 10x our current load. We've designed the seams (Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` today, Kafka topics when we extract a service) so the path to microservices is open.

What makes it impactful for me is the breadth of problems I had to solve: an OTP + Magic Link + Google OAuth hybrid auth, a metered credit system with `@Transactional` + pessimistic locking, a Spring Batch lead-discovery pipeline that scrapes public sources and enriches via LLM, a Gmail PubSub webhook system that classifies replies and advances the pipeline stage automatically, idempotent Stripe webhook handling, and a real-time notification fan-out across email/WhatsApp/Telegram/push. We are at 99.94% monthly uptime, p95 180ms, and we process ~2.1M leads cumulatively.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Java 17 LTS, Spring Boot 3.2.x, monolithic layered architecture
- PostgreSQL 15 + Redis 7, HikariCP, Spring Batch, Spring Security 6
- Multi-channel notification fan-out, idempotent Stripe webhooks
- Gmail PubSub webhook, AI outreach with LLM gateway
- 3,200 orgs / 50K users / 99.94% uptime / p95 180ms

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why monolith over microservices — wasn't that risky?
2. Walk me through one feature end-to-end.
3. What's the team size and what part did you personally own?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. We evaluated microservices in week 1. The cost — operational overhead, distributed transactions, network latency, ops surface — is only justified at our expected scale by mid-2027. We chose a clean modular monolith with bounded contexts (`com.acquisitionos.leads`, `.outreach`, `.meetings`, `.billing`, `.auth`, `.ai`) and Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` as the in-process bus. When we lift `ai` or `outreach` out, we'll swap the in-process listener for a Kafka consumer with no contract change.
2. Take `POST /api/outreach/send` — `JwtAuthenticationFilter` validates the JWT, sets `SecurityContext`, hits `OutreachController.send()` (`@PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER')")`, `@Valid SendDto`), which calls `OutreachService.send()` (`@Transactional(REPEATABLE_READ)` — deduct credits, persist message as SENT, enqueue to `MessageDeliveryService`), which publishes `OutboundMessageEvent`; `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` picks it up and dispatches to the right channel (Gmail/WhatsApp/Telegram) via a `ChannelRouter`. Returns 202 Accepted. The actual SMTP send is async; we record the SMTP message-id; a bounce webhook later marks the message as BOUNCED.
3. Team of 6: 2 backend (I'm the senior), 2 frontend, 1 QA, 1 PM. I personally owned auth (OTP/Magic Link/Google OAuth/MFA), payments (Stripe checkout + webhooks + invoices), the credit metering system, the AI outreach pipeline, the audit logging AOP aspect, and the deployment + observability setup. The other backend engineer owned the lead discovery + scraping + scoring engine and the meeting/calendar module.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Saying "I built everything" — every interviewer discounts this
- Saying "we used microservices" when the project is a monolith
- Quoting numbers without unit (e.g. "180 latency")
- Mentioning Next.js / Node as the backend
- Forgetting to mention external integrations (Stripe, Google)

---

### Q1-2: What is AcquisitionOS and what problem does it solve
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
AcquisitionOS is a B2B SaaS platform for AI-powered client acquisition. Sales teams today use 5–6 disconnected tools — a lead scraper, an email outreach tool, a CRM, a calendar scheduler, a pipeline manager, an analytics dashboard — with no closed loop between outreach and revenue. The data lives in silos; the rep spends 60% of their day switching context; there's no AI-driven prioritisation; nobody knows which outreach variant actually closed deals.

AcquisitionOS unifies the entire funnel. A user inputs a niche ("dentists in Mumbai") and our **Lead Discovery Pipeline** (Spring Batch + scraping workers + Google Places / LinkedIn enrichment + AI scoring) returns enriched leads with email, phone, social, revenue estimate, and a 0–100 quality score. The user picks leads, our `OutreachGeneratorService` calls the LLM with a templated prompt + lead context to generate 3 email variants, deducts credits (the platform's internal metered currency), and stores them. The user sends via Gmail SMTP (OAuth'd per-user) or Twilio WhatsApp with open/click tracking. Replies come back via Gmail PubSub / Twilio webhook → **Reply Intelligence** classifies intent (interested / not-now / unsubscribe) and auto-advances the lead stage in the **Pipeline**. When the lead says yes, **Meeting Scheduling** reads Google Calendar free/busy, proposes 3 slots, books a calendar invite. A `@Scheduled` job fires 24h / 1h reminders. Deals close in the Kanban pipeline, billing gets audited, the loop is closed.

The product is sold as a SaaS subscription (Free / Pro ₹1,599/mo / Elite ₹5,199/mo) with metered credits for AI actions. We're at 3,200 paying orgs, ~50K users, 2.1M leads processed, ~28K outreach emails/day, 99.94% monthly uptime, p95 180ms API latency.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- B2B SaaS, AI-powered client acquisition, unified funnel
- Lead Discovery Pipeline (Spring Batch), AI Scoring Engine
- Credit metering system (per-action cost)
- Gmail PubSub reply classification, Reply Intelligence
- Multi-channel: Gmail, WhatsApp, Telegram, push
- 3,200 orgs / 50K users / 2.1M leads / p95 180ms

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Who is the ICP — what kind of sales team?
2. How is the AI used exactly — is it GPT-4, Gemini, both?
3. What's your competitive moat vs Apollo.io / Outreach.io?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. ICP is small and mid-size B2B sales teams (5–30 reps) in services verticals — dental clinics, real estate brokerages, boutique SaaS agencies, marketing consultancies. They have a sales process but no SDR team to run it manually.
2. We use a provider-agnostic LLM gateway (`AiService` with `OpenAiClient` and `GeminiClient` implementations, picked by config). For outreach generation we use Gemini 1.5 Flash (cost-efficient, low latency); for lead scoring we use Gemini 1.5 Pro (better reasoning); for reply intent classification we use a smaller Gemini Flash with few-shot examples. We cache prompt+lead-hash → response in Redis for 24h to cut LLM cost by ~30%.
3. Two moats: (1) the unified closed loop — most competitors solve one piece, we own the whole funnel end-to-end which means the AI sees the full history (which outreach variant led to which reply led to which meeting led to which deal) and can train better recommendations; (2) the Indian-market focus — pricing in INR, GST-compliant invoicing, WhatsApp-first outreach (Indian buyers prefer WhatsApp over email), local niche templates.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Listing features without explaining the *problem* they solve
- Saying "AI" without specifying which model
- Skipping the pricing/business model (interviewers want to see you understand the business)
- Quoting scale numbers without explaining what they mean operationally

---

### Q1-3: What was your role and contribution
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
My official title is Senior Backend Engineer. I'm one of two backend engineers in a team of six (2 backend, 2 frontend, 1 QA, 1 PM). I joined at the design phase and have owned ~70% of the backend codebase since.

Specifically, I owned end-to-end: the auth subsystem (OTP, Magic Link, Google OAuth2 with Spring Security 6, MFA with TOTP, JWT stateless sessions, refresh-token rotation, brute-force lockout, audit logging); the payments subsystem (Stripe Checkout, Stripe webhooks with signature verification + idempotency, subscription lifecycle, credit-addon fulfilment, invoice generation with PDF service, GST-compliant invoicing for India); the credit metering system (atomic deduct with `@Transactional` + pessimistic lock, monthly reset via `@Scheduled` cron, rollover logic, plan-based entitlement gates); the AI outreach pipeline (LLM gateway with Resilience4j circuit breaker + retry + bulkhead, prompt templating with MapStruct DTOs, response caching in Redis); the audit logging AOP aspect (Spring AOP `@Aspect` intercepting service-layer methods, async write to audit table via Kafka); the deployment + observability setup (Docker, AWS ECS Fargate, GitHub Actions, Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + OpenTelemetry); and the Stripe webhook + Gmail PubSub + Twilio webhook receivers (idempotent, signature-verified, queue-backed).

What I didn't own — the other backend engineer did: the lead discovery + scraping engine (Spring Batch jobs, scraping workers, proxy rotation), the lead scoring model training (he partnered with our PM who has ML background), and the meeting/calendar module (Google Calendar API, free/busy optimisation, reminder scheduling).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Senior Backend Engineer, 70% backend ownership
- Spring Security 6, JWT, OTP, Magic Link, MFA TOTP, Google OAuth2
- Stripe webhooks idempotency + signature verification
- Credit metering with `@Transactional` + pessimistic lock
- Resilience4j circuit breaker around LLM gateway
- Spring AOP audit aspect, Docker / AWS ECS / GitHub Actions / Prometheus

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. How did you split work between the two backend engineers?
2. What's one piece you wish you'd done differently?
3. How did you handle code review across the backend team?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. We split along bounded contexts. I took `auth`, `billing`, `ai`, `outreach`, `notifications`, `infra` (cross-cutting + deployment). He took `leads`, `discovery`, `scraping`, `meetings`, `pipeline`. We agreed on interfaces (Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` events + a `DomainEvent` sealed interface) and reviewed each other's PRs. We did a "context ownership" doc so anyone joining knows who to ping for which module.
2. The credit metering system. I built it with a single `credit_balance` row updated under `@Transactional` + `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` — works perfectly at 3,200 tenants, but at 100K tenants every credit deduction will hit the same row for that user → contention. I'd redesign with a `credit_ledger` (append-only) + a materialised balance cache + a daily reconciliation job, exactly the way a bank ledger works. That's an answer I'll give if asked "what would you do differently" — and I'd honestly say I'm planning to refactor in Q2.
3. Two-eyes rule — every PR needs approval from the other backend engineer. We use GitHub PRs with CODEOWNERS files per bounded context; SonarQube quality gate must pass; integration tests (Testcontainers PG + Redis + WireMock for Stripe/Google) must pass; coverage cannot drop below 75% line. For infra changes (Terraform, Dockerfile, GitHub Actions), I require both backend engineers + the devops contractor.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Saying "I was the lead" / "I managed the team" — you're an IC, not a manager
- Not knowing what you didn't own — looks fake
- Overestimating ownership % (anything above 80% sounds invented)
- Mentioning frontend tasks unless explicitly asked

### Q1-4: What was the team size and your responsibilities
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Team of 6 — 2 backend engineers (I'm the senior), 2 frontend engineers (React 18 + TypeScript 5), 1 QA engineer (Playwright + Vitest), 1 product manager. We worked in 2-week sprints with a kanban board and shipped a minor release every 4–6 weeks.

My responsibilities spanned the backend vertically: design (I wrote most of the architecture decision records — ADRs — for the credit metering, the webhook idempotency pattern, the AI gateway circuit breaker, the audit AOP pattern), implementation (Java + Spring Boot code), testing (JUnit 5 + Mockito unit tests, `@DataJpaTest` slice tests with H2, `@SpringBootTest` integration tests with Testcontainers PG + Redis, WireMock for Stripe / Google / Twilio / LLM), deployment (Docker build, ECS Fargate task definitions, GitHub Actions CI/CD with blue/green deploys, rollback strategy), observability (Micrometer metrics exposed to Prometheus, custom business meters like `credits.spent`, `leads.discovered`, `outreach.sent`; OpenTelemetry tracing; Loki for logs; Sentry for errors), and on-call (we do a 1-week rotation between the two backend engineers; PagerDuty + Discord alerts).

The other backend engineer focused on the data plane: the lead discovery + scraping engine (Spring Batch chunk jobs, proxy rotation, scraping workers), the lead scoring model (partnering with the PM who has ML background), and the meeting/calendar module (Google Calendar API, free/busy optimisation, reminder scheduling).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Team of 6: 2 backend, 2 frontend, 1 QA, 1 PM
- ADRs (Architecture Decision Records)
- JUnit 5 + Mockito + Testcontainers + WireMock
- GitHub Actions CI/CD, blue/green deploy, rollback
- Micrometer + Prometheus + Loki + OpenTelemetry + Sentry
- PagerDuty on-call rotation

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. How did you handle disagreements with the other backend engineer?
2. Walk me through your CI/CD pipeline.
3. What was your on-call experience like — any production incidents?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. We disagreed on whether to use Kafka or stick with Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher`. He wanted Kafka for "future-proofing"; I argued that adding Kafka before we needed it would multiply operational cost (brokers, schema registry, consumer lag monitoring) for zero current benefit. We resolved it by writing an ADR with a decision rule: "Use Spring Events until a context publishes >1K events/sec or needs to be extracted to its own service". We are nowhere near that threshold today. We re-evaluate every quarter.
2. GitHub Actions workflow: (1) Maven build + unit tests (parallel across modules), (2) integration tests with Testcontainers (PG + Redis + Kafka), (3) SonarQube quality gate, (4) Maven package → Docker build with layered jar (separate `dependencies` layer from `application` layer for cache reuse), (5) push to ECR with semantic version tag, (6) deploy to ECS Fargate staging via blue/green — new tasks come up alongside old, ALB health checks pass, traffic shifts 10% → 50% → 100% over 15 minutes, (7) if any 5xx spike → auto-rollback. Manual prod-deploy button after staging smoke tests. Total CI time: ~7 minutes.
3. We had one P0 in the last 6 months — Stripe webhook handler crashed under a sudden burst of 600 webhooks in 2 minutes (Stripe retries aggressively when it sees a 500). Root cause: a transactional boundary mistake — I had `@Transactional` on the whole handler instead of per-event-processing; one bad webhook held a DB connection for 30s while HikariCP exhausted at 20 connections. Fix: split the handler into "ingest" (just persist raw webhook, return 200 to Stripe) + "process" (async via Kafka consumer, per-event transaction). Added a HikariCP alarm at 80% utilisation. We added a load test that fires 1000 concurrent webhooks as a regression test. Postmortem published to the team.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- "We were 50 people" — sounds invented for a 9-month-old product
- "I did all the on-call" — unhealthy team signal
- Skipping CI/CD details — every senior interview drills this
- Saying "no incidents" — looks fake; mention the postmortem honestly

### Q1-5: What is the tech stack and why did you choose it
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Backend: **Java 17 LTS** because of records (immutable DTOs), sealed classes (domain event hierarchies), pattern matching for switch (clean service dispatch), mature GC options (we use G1 with -Xmx2g), virtual threads preview (we tested with `Thread.ofVirtual()` for some IO-heavy paths but kept platform threads for stability). Spring Boot 3.2.x because it requires Java 17 (no legacy), ships Spring 6 + Security 6 + Data JPA 3.2, has native support if we want to go GraalVM later, and has first-class observability via Micrometer. We use Spring Web MVC (servlet stack, one thread per request) rather than WebFlux because our workload is CRUD-heavy with occasional long-poll (SSE), not high-concurrency reactive — the team has stronger servlet skills and debugging reactive code at 3am is harder.

Persistence: **Hibernate 6 via Spring Data JPA** — gives us repository abstraction, query derivation, Specifications for dynamic queries, and we control N+1 with `@EntityGraph` and `@BatchSize`. **PostgreSQL 15** because of JSONB (we store tags, settings, AI reasoning as JSONB), GIN indexes for full-text search on leads, CTE + window functions for analytics dashboards, mature replication (Multi-AZ + 2 read replicas), and a strong ecosystem. **Flyway** for migrations because versioned SQL beats Liquibase's XML for readability.

Cache + locks + rate-limit: **Redis 7** in cluster mode (3 shards, 1 replica each) for: (a) HTTP session + JWT allowlist cache, (b) sliding-window rate-limit (`ZADD` + `ZRANGEBYSCORE`), (c) distributed lock via `SET NX PX` for cron dedup, (d) LLM response cache (prompt+lead hash → response, TTL 24h), (e) leaderboard sorted sets, (f) pub/sub for cache invalidation.

Background jobs: **Spring Batch** for the lead discovery pipeline (chunk-oriented: scrape 50 → enrich → score → persist, repeat with restart capability), **`@Async` + `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`** for short-lived fan-out (notification dispatch), **`@Scheduled`** for cron-style jobs (subscription renewals, reminder polling, monthly credit reset). We use a `job_state` table in Postgres for durable state so a crashed task can resume.

External integrations: **WebClient** (non-blocking, fluent, integrates with Resilience4j) for Stripe / Google / Twilio / LLM calls. **Resilience4j** for circuit breaker (10% failure rate → open for 30s), retry (exponential backoff with jitter), bulkhead (limit concurrent calls per integration), time limiter (5s for LLM, 10s for Google).

Testing: **JUnit 5 + Mockito + AssertJ** for units, `@WebMvcTest` / `@DataJpaTest` for slice tests, `@SpringBootTest` with Testcontainers (PostgreSQL + Redis + Kafka) for integration, WireMock for Stripe / Google / Twilio / OpenAI contract tests. 78% line coverage, 64% branch.

Observability: Micrometer + Prometheus + Grafana for metrics, OpenTelemetry + Tempo for traces, Loki for logs, Sentry for errors. We expose custom business meters (credits.spent, leads.discovered, outreach.sent) alongside JVM/Hikari/HTTP meters.

Infra: Docker (Eclipse Temurin JRE 17-jammy base), AWS ECS Fargate (4 tasks, 2 vCPU/4GiB each, ALB), RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ + 2 read replicas, ElastiCache Redis cluster, S3 + CloudFront for attachments/invoices, GitHub Actions CI/CD with blue/green deploys.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Java 17 (records, sealed, pattern matching, G1 GC)
- Spring Boot 3.2.x, Spring Web MVC (not WebFlux), Spring Data JPA, Hibernate 6
- PostgreSQL 15 (JSONB, GIN, CTE, Multi-AZ + read replicas), Flyway
- Redis 7 cluster: session, rate-limit ZSET, distributed lock, LLM cache, pub/sub
- Spring Batch, @Async ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, @Scheduled
- WebClient + Resilience4j (CB, retry, bulkhead, time limiter)
- JUnit 5 + Mockito + AssertJ + Testcontainers + WireMock
- Micrometer + Prometheus + Grafana + OpenTelemetry + Loki + Sentry
- Docker + ECS Fargate + RDS + ElastiCache + S3 + GitHub Actions

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why Spring Web MVC over WebFlux?
2. Why Redis cluster mode over a single Redis with sentinel?
3. Why ECS Fargate over EKS or Lambda?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Our workload is CRUD-heavy (most requests are <50ms DB read), with occasional SSE for live notifications. WebFlux's benefit shows at >10K concurrent connections holding open — we don't have that profile. The team is also stronger with servlet stack; debugging reactive back-pressure issues at 3am is brutal. We tested virtual threads in 3.2.x for one IO-heavy path (the LLM gateway) — got 30% throughput improvement without reactive complexity. If we ever need reactive, the LLM gateway is the first candidate to extract as a separate reactive service.
2. Single Redis with sentinel works up to ~10K ops/sec, but our rate-limit + LLM cache + session cache combined already hit 8K ops/sec at peak. Cluster mode gives us horizontal scaling (3 shards = 24K ops/sec headroom) and built-in failover. The downside — no cross-slot transactions — doesn't affect us because each key is independent.
3. ECS Fargate over EKS: we don't need K8s features (custom schedulers, operators, CRDs), and operating EKS is a part-time job for one engineer. Fargate is serverless containers — we don't manage the control plane. ECS Fargate over Lambda: our requests are not cold-start friendly (DB connection warmup is 200ms) and we have long-running Spring Batch jobs that don't fit Lambda's 15min limit. If we ever extract a service to be event-driven and short-lived, Lambda is on the table.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Listing tools without explaining *why*
- Saying "we used Kafka" when the team actually uses Spring Events
- Saying "microservices" when the project is a monolith
- Skipping the *testing* and *observability* parts of the stack — interviewers notice

### Q1-6: What was the most challenging part of building this
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
The hardest part was the **credit metering system** — the platform's internal metered currency that gates every paid AI action. Every paid feature (lead discovery, outreach generation, deep analysis, website scraping) costs credits; every plan ships a monthly allowance (Free 50 / Pro 500 / Elite 2000); unused monthly credits rollover up to 2x the monthly allowance; addon packs (₹499 / ₹1,999 / ₹3,499) can be purchased; credits must be atomic, auditable, refundable, and survive crashes.

The naive implementation (`UPDATE credit_balance SET balance = balance - cost WHERE user_id = ?`) has a race condition: two concurrent requests both read balance=10, both deduct 5, both write 5 — we lost 5 credits. The fix was `@Transactional(isolation=REPEATABLE_READ) + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the balance row, plus an append-only `credit_ledger` table that records every movement with `reference_id` (idempotency key) so we can replay and reconcile. We also added a `@Version` optimistic lock on the User entity as a defence-in-depth — but the pessimistic lock is the primary guard for high-contention users.

The next problem was partial failure: if we deduct credits and the AI call fails, we must refund. We use a `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` — when the `CreditsDeductedEvent` commits, we trigger the AI call. If the AI call throws, a `CreditRefundService` issues a compensating ledger entry. We use the **Saga pattern** (choreography, not orchestration) for this: `OutreachGenerationRequested → CreditsDeducted → AiCallSucceeded → OutreachGenerated` OR `AiCallFailed → CreditsRefunded → OutreachFailed`. Each step has a compensating action; each is idempotent (keyed by `reference_id` in the ledger).

The hardest sub-problem was the monthly reset with rollover. On the 1st of every month, a `@Scheduled` cron job iterates all users, resets `credits_monthly` to the plan's allowance, computes the rollover (min(current_unused, 2 × monthly_allowance)), and writes a new `credit_ledger` row of type "rollover-grant" + a "monthly-reset" row. We made this idempotent (the ledger has a unique key on `(user_id, period_start, type)` so the job can be re-run safely). For 3,200 users it runs in ~40 seconds — we batch in groups of 100, parallel via `@Async` with a `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` of size 4. At 100K users we'll move this to a Spring Batch job partitioned by `user_id % 10`.

The last sub-problem was audit and refund: every ledger entry has `action`, `cost`, `balance_after`, `reference_id`, `metadata` (JSONB — lead id, message id, etc.). Customer support can refund a credit by issuing a `credit_refund` ledger entry that links back to the original `credit_deduct` entry via `reference_id`. We have a daily reconciliation job that recomputes `SUM(credit_ledger.cost) FROM ledger WHERE user_id = ?` and compares to `credit_balance.balance` — if they drift, we alert (this caught a bug once when a developer forgot the `@TransactionalEventListener` phase and refunded outside the transaction).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Atomic credit deduction with `@Transactional(REPEATABLE_READ) + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
- Append-only `credit_ledger` table, idempotency via `reference_id`
- Saga pattern (choreography) with `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)`
- Compensating transactions, idempotent refund
- `@Version` optimistic lock as defence-in-depth
- `@Scheduled` monthly reset cron, parallel via `@Async ThreadPoolTaskExecutor`
- Daily reconciliation job: SUM(ledger) vs balance, alert on drift

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why pessimistic lock over optimistic lock?
2. What's the failure mode if the AI call hangs and the credit is deducted?
3. How would you scale this to 100K users?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Optimistic lock with `@Version` works well for low contention — but a power user running 20 outreach generations in parallel will hit `OptimisticLockException` retries constantly. Pessimistic lock with `SELECT FOR UPDATE` serialises their requests cleanly. We use optimistic lock as the *fallback* in case the pessimistic lock times out (LockTimeoutException → retry once with optimistic, then fail the request with a 503).
2. The AI call is wrapped in Resilience4j `TimeLimiter` (5 seconds). On timeout, we throw `AiCallTimeoutException`, the `@TransactionalEventListener` catches it, publishes `AiCallFailedEvent`, the credit refund saga kicks in. If the AI call *succeeded* on the provider side but we timed out reading the response (rare), the idempotency key (lead-hash + prompt-hash) lets us retry safely — the second call hits the LLM cache in Redis.
3. At 100K users, the monthly reset job runs on a Spring Batch partitioned by `user_id % 10` — 10 parallel partitions, each processes 10K users. The `credit_balance` row lock contention grows linearly with the user's request rate, so a user issuing 100 deductions/sec would saturate the row — we'd move to a Redis-cached balance with periodic flush to the ledger (write-behind pattern), and the ledger becomes the source of truth with the cache as the read-optimised projection.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Skipping the race condition discussion
- Saying "we used transactions" without specifying isolation level
- Forgetting to mention audit/refund — credits are real money
- Not knowing how you'd scale it

### Q1-7: What would you do differently if you rebuilt it
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Three things I'd do differently, in order of impact:

**1. Event-sourced the credit ledger from day one.** Today, `credit_balance` is a mutable row updated under `SELECT FOR UPDATE`. At 3,200 tenants this is fine, but at 100K it will be a bottleneck. I'd event-source from day one: the `credit_ledger` is the source of truth (append-only), and `credit_balance` is a materialised projection recomputed from the ledger. We already write the ledger — we just don't read from it for the balance. The fix is to add a daily reconciliation that drifts the balance back to the ledger sum and a Redis cached balance that's invalidated on each ledger write. I'm planning this for Q2.

**2. Owned the multi-tenancy story earlier.** We added `org_id` to every table in month 4, but the early code assumed single-tenant. Retrofitting required touching every query, every repository, every index. We use Hibernate `@Filter("tenantFilter")` for the data plane but it's leaky — a developer who forgets `@FilterDef` exposes cross-tenant data. I'd introduce multi-tenancy at the schema level (schema-per-tenant or `tenant_id` column with a Hibernate filter applied automatically by an aspect) from week one. This is the kind of "do it now, thank yourself later" decision that costs 10x to retrofit.

**3. Built the AI gateway as a separate module from day one.** Today the LLM calls are scattered across `OutreachGenerator`, `LeadScoringEngine`, `ReplyClassifier`, `MeetingAssistant` — each calls `AiService` which delegates to `OpenAiClient` or `GeminiClient`. The scattering means prompt versioning is messy (we version per caller, not centrally), cost tracking is per-caller, and circuit breaking is per-caller. I'd build a single `AiGateway` that owns: prompt templates (versioned in a `prompt_template` table), provider routing (cost/latency-based), caching (Redis with prompt+input hash), cost tracking (per user, per feature), circuit breaking (per provider, not per caller), and fallback chains (Gemini → OpenAI → local model). This is exactly the kind of internal platform that pays back fast at scale.

Bonus: I'd also adopt **OpenTelemetry tracing from day one** rather than retrofitting it in month 5. Retrofitting meant instrumenting ~40 controllers and ~80 service methods; doing it from day one would have been a one-line `application.yml` change.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Event sourcing for credit ledger, materialised projection
- Multi-tenancy: schema-per-tenant or Hibernate `@Filter("tenantFilter")`
- AI Gateway abstraction (prompt versioning, provider routing, caching, cost tracking, circuit breaker per provider)
- OpenTelemetry from day one vs retrofit
- Write-behind cache for hot rows

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why event sourcing for credits specifically?
2. Have you ever done event sourcing in production?
3. What's the cost of retrofitting OpenTelemetry?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Credits are a financial ledger — append-only semantics fit naturally. We already write the ledger; we just don't read from it for the balance. The balance becomes a projection. Event sourcing also gives us replay (recompute balance from any point in time), audit (every movement is recorded), and time-travel debugging ("show me user X's credits on 2025-08-15 at noon"). The trade-off is eventual consistency — the balance is a cached projection; for the rare case where we need strict consistency (e.g. right after a refund), we read the ledger sum directly.
2. Yes, in a previous project — a payment ledger for a fintech app. We used Kafka as the event log and a CQRS read-model in Postgres. The lessons: (a) idempotency keys are mandatory (consumers redeliver), (b) schema evolution is hard (we used Avro + schema registry), (c) replays are expensive (we kept 30 days of events in Kafka, older events in S3). For AcquisitionOS credits, the volume is much lower (~3,200 ledger writes/day), so Postgres as the event log is fine — no Kafka needed yet.
3. Retrofitting OpenTelemetry took ~3 days: adding the agent, instrumenting controllers and services manually, wiring up Tempo as the backend, and adding trace propagation to WebClient calls. The harder part was educating the team to add `@WithSpan` annotations to new code. From day one it would have been 30 minutes (auto-instrumentation covers 80%).

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Saying "nothing" — looks like you can't reflect
- Listing 10 things — looks unfocused
- Picking something the interviewer can prove you're wrong about (e.g. "I'd use MongoDB" when you've never used it)

### Q1-8: How long did it take to build
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Design phase: 6 weeks (architecture decisions, schema design, ADRs, spike on Spring Batch for lead discovery, OAuth flow design for Google Calendar, Stripe webhook idempotency design).

MVP build: 4 months — we shipped with auth (OTP + Magic Link + Google OAuth), lead discovery (single niche: dental clinics in Mumbai), pipeline (Kanban with 5 stages), outreach (Gmail SMTP only, no AI), basic credit metering, Stripe checkout (Pro/Elite), and the admin feedback panel. MVP served 30 beta customers.

Production hardening: 3 months — added MFA, refresh-token rotation, audit logging, Resilience4j circuit breakers on every external call, Spring Batch for the discovery pipeline, AI outreach (LLM gateway), Gmail PubSub reply intelligence, Twilio WhatsApp, Telegram bots, read replicas, Redis cluster, blue/green deploys, Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + OpenTelemetry, daily reconciliation jobs.

Iterative releases: ongoing — we ship a minor release every 4–6 weeks. Recent additions: AI scoring engine, sequence enrolment (email sequences), meeting scheduling with Google Calendar, white-label org branding, GST-compliant invoicing, GDPR data export/delete workflows.

Total from zero to public launch: ~7 months. We then went from 30 beta customers to 3,200 paying orgs over the next ~9 months through product-led growth (free tier → paid upgrade) and a small sales team.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- 6-week design phase with ADRs and spikes
- 4-month MVP, 30 beta customers
- 3-month production hardening (security, observability, scale, retries)
- Continuous 4-6 week release cadence
- Product-led growth Free → Paid

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. What was the first thing you shipped in MVP?
2. What did you cut from MVP that you regret?
3. How did you measure MVP success?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Auth + lead discovery (single niche: dental clinics in Mumbai, scraped from Google Places) + basic pipeline (Kanban) + Gmail outreach (no AI) + Stripe checkout. We had ~10 endpoints. The PM ran weekly design partner calls with 5 beta customers; their feedback shaped the next 3 months.
2. Audit logging. We shipped MVP without it because "we'll add it later". Then a paying customer reported a credit discrepancy and we had no trail. We added it the next week as a Spring AOP aspect on every service-layer mutation — took 2 days. Should have been there from day 1. Lesson: any financial system needs audit from day one, not "later".
3. Three metrics: (a) activation — did the user discover at least 10 leads in the first session (proxy for "they got value"); (b) retention — did they return within 7 days; (c) conversion — did any free-tier user upgrade to paid within 30 days. Our activation was 68%, retention 42%, conversion 8% — industry-standard for SaaS. The PM tracked these weekly; we shipped features that moved activation first.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Saying "6 months to 1M users" — sounds invented
- Skipping MVP definition (looks like you don't know what MVP means)
- Not mentioning what you cut

### Q1-9: Is it live in production? How many users
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Yes — live in production since January 2026. We have ~3,200 paying organizations (Pro or Elite — Free tier has ~8,000 more orgs but we don't count them as paying), ~50,000 monthly active users across those orgs, and we've processed ~2.1M leads cumulatively (we crossed 1M in May). We send ~28K outreach emails/day, ~9,500 AI requests/day, and process ~3,000 Stripe webhook events/day.

Operationally: 99.94% monthly uptime SLA (we contractually promise 99.9% to Pro and 99.95% to Elite). p50 API latency 65ms, p95 180ms, p99 540ms. Peak ~1,200 requests/sec during Indian business hours. Single PostgreSQL primary (db.r6g.large) + 2 read replicas, Redis cluster (3 shards, 1 replica each), 4 ECS Fargate tasks behind an ALB, autoscaling on CPU > 70% + ALB request count > 1000.

The product is profitable (not break-even) as of July 2026, driven by the credit addon packs (₹499 / ₹1,999 / ₹3,499) which sell well to power users. We have a 4.3% monthly churn (industry standard for SMB SaaS) and a 92% net revenue retention (expansion via addon packs offsets churn).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- 3,200 paying orgs, 50K MAU, 2.1M leads cumulative
- 28K outreach emails/day, 9,500 AI requests/day, 3,000 Stripe webhooks/day
- 99.94% uptime SLA (99.9% Pro, 99.95% Elite contractual)
- p50 65ms / p95 180ms / p99 540ms
- db.r6g.large primary + 2 read replicas, Redis cluster 3 shards
- 4 ECS Fargate tasks, ALB, autoscaling on CPU + request count
- Profitable since July 2026, 4.3% monthly churn, 92% NRR

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. How do you measure uptime?
2. What's the biggest outage you've had?
3. How do you measure p99 — over what window?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Uptime = (total minutes - error minutes) / total minutes where "error minute" = any minute with >1% 5xx rate from the ALB. We measure with a 1-minute ping from 3 regions (Mumbai, Singapore, us-east-1) via UptimeRobot + a synthetic check that does a real login + lead list call every minute. The synthetic is more reliable than ping because the ALB returns 200 even if the app is dead.
2. A 23-minute outage in March 2026. We deployed a Hibernate config change that enabled second-level cache for the `Lead` entity without configuring a provider — Hibernate threw on startup, the new ECS tasks crashed, the ALB drained them, but the old tasks had already been terminated. Blue/green deploy should have caught this but the health check passed (the app started, then crashed 30 seconds later) — the 30s window was within the health check interval. Fix: (1) longer health check grace period (60s), (2) Hibernate config validation in CI (we added a `@SpringBootTest` context-load test).
3. p99 is measured over a 10-minute sliding window per endpoint, computed by Micrometer and exposed to Prometheus. We use 10 minutes rather than 1 minute because a single slow request (e.g. a complex analytics query) shouldn't dominate the metric. For business reporting we also compute daily p99 over a 24h window.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Quoting fake numbers (e.g. "10 million users")
- Saying "no outages" — looks fake
- Saying p99 = 50ms (sub-millisecond p99 looks like you're not measuring)
- Not knowing what "p99 over what window" means

### Q1-10: What metrics show the success of this product
**DIFFICULTY:** Easy
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
We track four layers of metrics: business, product, system, and engineering.

**Business metrics (the PM owns these, I track them in dashboards):** MRR (₹4.2M/month, growing 12% MoM), ARPU (₹1,315/org/month — pulled down by Free tier; Pro ARPU is ₹1,899, Elite ARPU is ₹5,800 with addon packs), LTV/CAC ratio (3.4x — healthy for SMB SaaS, target is >3), gross margin (84% — the LLM cost is the biggest COGS at ~$4,200/month), NRR (92% — expansion via addons), churn (4.3% monthly logo, 2.1% revenue — revenue churn is lower because power users churn less).

**Product metrics:** Activation rate (68% — user discovers 10+ leads in first session), D7 retention (42%), D30 retention (28%), free → paid conversion (8%), feature adoption (Pro users use 4.2 features on average, Elite users 7.8), AI outreach send rate (32% of generated emails are actually sent by the user — we want to push this up with better templates).

**System metrics:** Uptime (99.94% monthly), p50/p95/p99 API latency (65/180/540ms), error rate (0.06% — mostly 400s), DB query p95 (40ms — most queries hit an index), Redis hit ratio (94%), Kafka consumer lag (under 50 messages steady-state, spikes to 5K during batch jobs), HikariCP utilisation (peaks at 65% — comfortable).

**Engineering metrics:** CI duration (7 min), deploy frequency (3 deploys/week), lead time (PR merge → prod: 1.4 days median), MTTR (28 min — most incidents are config rollbacks), change failure rate (8% — slightly above the DORA "elite" 5% threshold), code coverage (78% line, 64% branch), SonarQube technical debt ratio (4.2% — under our 5% gate), PR review time (median 6 hours).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- MRR, ARPU, LTV/CAC, NRR, churn (logo vs revenue)
- Gross margin, COGS (LLM cost)
- D7/D30 retention, activation rate, free → paid conversion
- p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, Redis hit ratio, HikariCP utilisation
- DORA metrics: deploy frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate
- Code coverage 78% line / 64% branch, SonarQube debt ratio 4.2%

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. How do you reduce LLM cost without hurting quality?
2. What's your DORA "elite" status target?
3. How do you measure developer velocity?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Three levers: (a) model routing — we use Gemini 1.5 Flash for outreach generation (cost $0.075/M input tokens) and Gemini 1.5 Pro only for lead scoring (better reasoning, $1.25/M); (b) caching — we cache prompt+lead-hash → response in Redis for 24h, hitting 30% cache ratio on outreach (users often regenerate for similar leads); (c) prompt compression — we use a "few-shot condensed" template (3 examples instead of 8) with a system message that's loaded once per session, cutting input tokens by 40%. Combined, our LLM cost is $0.44 per outreach email sent — well below the $0.99 the user pays in credits.
2. DORA "elite" is: deploy frequency >1/day, lead time <1 hour, MTTR <1 hour, change failure rate <5%. We're "high" today (3 deploys/week, 1.4 days lead time, 28 min MTTR, 8% CFR). The next leap is "elite" via: (a) automated canary deploys to get to daily, (b) trunk-based development + feature flags to cut lead time to hours, (c) better canary analysis to catch failures earlier (lower MTTR + CFR).
3. We use LinearB for engineering metrics: PR size median (84 lines), review time median (6 hours), cycle time (3.2 days — from "in progress" to "merged"), shipping frequency (2.3 PRs/engineer/week). The PM cares about cycle time; I care about PR size (large PRs = harder to review = more bugs).

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Quoting MRR without context (₹4.2M is good but explain MoM growth)
- Saying "we use DORA" without knowing the four metrics
- Mixing up "churn" definitions (logo vs revenue)
- Quoting LLM cost without the per-unit economics

### Q1-11: Walk me through one feature end-to-end
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Let me walk you through `POST /api/leads/discover` — the lead discovery kick-off endpoint. This is a good example because it touches every layer and shows the async pattern.

**Request hits the ALB** → TLS termination → forwards to one of 4 ECS tasks. The Spring Boot app's `DispatcherServlet` matches the route to `LeadDiscoverController.discoverLeads(@Valid @RequestBody DiscoverDto dto, Principal principal)`.

**Security filter chain** (in order): `SecurityContextHolderFilter` → `HeaderWriterFilter` → `CorsFilter` (rejects if origin not allow-listed) → `RateLimitFilter` (Redis sliding-window: `ZADD rl:discover:{userId}:{ip} {now} {now}; ZREMRANGEBYSCORE ... {now-60s} {now}; ZCARD ...` — returns 429 with Retry-After if >20/min) → `JwtAuthenticationFilter` (verifies the HS256 JWT using `JwtDecoder` configured with the signing key from Secrets Manager, sets `SecurityContext.authentication` with the user's id, email, role, plan) → `AuditAspect` records the request → finally `DispatcherServlet` dispatches to the controller.

**Controller** (`LeadDiscoverController`): `@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/leads/discover") @Validated`. The method has `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('USER','ADMIN') and @creditGuard.hasCredits(principal, #dto.maxResults)")` — the `creditGuard` is a custom bean that peeks the credit balance; the `@PreAuthorize` runs *before* the service call so we fail fast if the user has no credits.

**Service** (`LeadService.discoverLeads(DiscoverDto, AuthUser)`): `@Transactional(isolation = REPEATABLE_READ, rollbackFor = Exception.class)`. Steps:
1. Idempotency check: `discoverJobRepository.findByRequestId(dto.requestId())` — if exists, return the existing job state (idempotent retry from a flaky client).
2. Plan entitlement: `entitlementService.check(user.plan(), "lead_discovery", dto.maxResults())` — Free plan caps at 10 leads, Pro at 50, Elite at 200. Throws `PlanEntitlementException` if exceeded.
3. Create `DiscoverJob` entity (status=PENDING, niche, location, maxResults, requestId, userId), persist via `discoverJobRepository.save()`.
4. Deduct credits atomically: `creditService.deduct(user.id(), LEAD_DISCOVERY_COST × dto.maxResults(), "discover", job.id())`. Internally: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on `credit_balance` row, check `balance >= cost`, `UPDATE balance = balance - cost`, append `credit_ledger` row, commit. If `balance < cost` → throw `InsufficientCreditsException` → triggers a rollback that also rolls back the DiscoverJob insert.
5. Publish `LeadDiscoveryRequestedEvent(jobId)` via `ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent()`. The event listener is `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution = true)` so it only fires after the transaction commits.
6. Return 202 Accepted with the job id.

**Async path** (separate thread from the `TaskExecutor`): `DiscoveryJobRunner.onApplicationEvent()` calls `leadDiscoveryService.discover(jobId)`. This is a Spring Batch job with chunk-oriented steps: scrape 50 candidates → enrich (Google Places + LinkedIn API via WebClient + Resilience4j circuit breaker) → score (LLM call) → batch insert via `leadRepository.saveAll()`. Spring Batch writes checkpoint state to the `job_state` table every 50 leads so a crash can resume.

**On completion**: `DiscoverJob.status = COMPLETED`, `LeadDiscoveryCompletedEvent` published → `NotificationService` pushes a notification (multi-channel: in-app via WebSocket, email, Telegram if connected). The user sees the leads in their UI via `GET /api/leads?filter=stage=discovered&jobId=...`.

**On failure**: `DiscoverJob.status = FAILED`, error message stored, `CreditRefundService.refund(jobId, "discover-failed")` issues a compensating ledger entry. Resilience4j retries with exponential backoff (1s, 4s, 16s) before declaring failure.

The whole flow is observable end-to-end: OpenTelemetry trace from controller → service → repository → external APIs (Google, LLM) → response, with span attributes for `userId`, `jobId`, `niche`, `credits.cost`.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- SecurityFilterChain: SecurityContextHolder, HeaderWriter, Cors, RateLimit, JwtAuth filters in order
- `@PreAuthorize` with custom `creditGuard` bean — fail fast before service
- `@Transactional(REPEATABLE_READ, rollbackFor = Exception.class)`
- Idempotency via `requestId` lookup
- Plan entitlement gate before DB write
- Credit deduct via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` + append-only ledger
- `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT, fallbackExecution=true)` for async dispatch
- Spring Batch chunk-oriented: scrape → enrich → score → saveAll, checkpoint every 50
- Resilience4j retry with exponential backoff + jitter
- OpenTelemetry trace end-to-end with span attributes

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. What happens if the user disconnects after sending the request?
2. How do you handle the case where the LLM score API is down?
3. Why REPEATABLE_READ isolation specifically?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. The request is async — the client gets 202 + jobId and can poll `GET /api/leads/discover/status/{jobId}`. If the client disconnects, the Spring Batch job continues; the user reconnects and polls. If the user kills the app, we still complete the job; the notification reaches them via email/Telegram. We use SSE for live updates — if the SSE connection drops, the client reconnects with `Last-Event-ID` and we replay missed events from a Kafka backlog (24h retention).
2. Resilience4j circuit breaker around the LLM call: at 10% failure rate, the circuit opens for 30s. During open state, we fall back to a heuristic score (rule-based: rating × niche_demand × revenue_estimate). When the circuit half-opens, we try one call; if it succeeds, we close. We log every circuit transition as a Prometheus counter. We also persist the heuristic score on the lead so the user sees *something* even during an outage.
3. We need REPEATABLE_READ because: (a) the credit deduction must see a stable view of the balance row (otherwise a concurrent deduct could read a stale balance and over-spend); (b) the DiscoverJob insert must be consistent with the credit ledger row we're about to insert. SERIALIZABLE would be stricter but slower (more aborts). READ_COMMITTED would let a concurrent request see an inconsistent balance. REPEATABLE_READ is the sweet spot — Postgres's MVCC implementation makes it nearly free.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Skipping the security filter chain (interviewer wants to hear it)
- Forgetting the credit deduct race condition
- Not mentioning async / event listener
- Saying "we just use @Transactional" without isolation level

### Q1-12: What would you not build again
**DIFFICULTY:** Hard
**CATEGORY TAG:** Project Introduction

**ANSWER:**
Three things I would not build again, in order of regret:

**1. Custom TOTP / MFA implementation.** We hand-rolled TOTP using `javax.crypto.Mac` and the RFC 6238 spec — 200 lines of code for secret generation, base32 encoding, time-step calculation, dynamic truncation. We did this because we wanted no extra dependency. Six months later we found two bugs: (a) our backup codes had a 32-bit entropy (4 random bytes — too low, brute-forceable in 4 days at 100 attempts/sec), (b) our clock drift tolerance was ±1 step but we didn't lock the user out after 5 failed MFA attempts. We fixed both, but if I redid this I'd use a library like `dev.samstevens.totp:totp` (or Spring Security's `GoogleAuthenticatorKey` integration if it shipped one — it doesn't, so a library is fine). The lesson: crypto code is the worst place to roll your own — use a vetted library, even if the dependency feels heavy.

**2. Custom audit log writer with Spring AOP + Kafka.** We have a `@AuditedAction` annotation and an `AuditAspect` that intercepts service-layer methods, serialises the arguments (with sensitive fields masked), and writes to Kafka topic `audit-events`, which a consumer writes to Postgres `audit_logs`. The aspect works, but it's leaky — developers forget to add `@AuditedAction` to new methods, and the aspect can't capture return values cleanly without `@Around` advice (which adds overhead). If I redid this I'd use a Hibernate `Interceptor` (or `@EntityListener` with `@PostPersist`, `@PostUpdate`, `@PostRemove`) — every entity mutation gets an audit row automatically, no annotation needed. We're actually migrating to this pattern in Q3 because the aspect approach doesn't scale to 200+ services.

**3. Hand-rolled rate limiter with Redis sorted sets.** We use `ZADD` + `ZREMRANGEBYSCORE` + `ZCARD` per request — works, but it's 3 Redis round-trips per request. We could have used `INCR` + `EXPIRE` (1 round-trip, approximate window) or a token-bucket Lua script (1 round-trip, exact). The 3 round-trips add ~6ms p99 latency to every protected endpoint. We're switching to a token-bucket Lua script in Q2.

Bonus: I'd also not write our own Stripe webhook signature verification. We use Stripe's `Webhook.constructEvent()` library — fine — but we initially wrote our own HMAC verification. Stripe changes the signature scheme (they did, to v2 signed payloads) and we'd have to keep up. Always use the vendor's library for crypto.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Don't roll your own crypto / TOTP — use vetted libraries
- Hibernate `Interceptor` / `@EntityListener` > AOP aspect for audit
- Token-bucket Lua script (1 Redis round-trip) > sliding window ZSET (3 round-trips)
- Vendor libraries for webhook signature verification

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why didn't you use a library for TOTP from the start?
2. How does the Hibernate Interceptor approach compare to the AOP approach?
3. Why is 3 Redis round-trips a problem when Redis is fast?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Honestly — I didn't think a 200-line implementation was risky. TOTP is RFC 6238, the algorithm is 20 lines, what could go wrong? Three things: (a) backup code entropy (we picked 4 bytes instead of 16), (b) clock drift window (we allowed ±1 step but no lockout), (c) constant-time comparison (we used `equals()` for backup codes — timing attack possible). All three were caught in a security audit. The lesson: even "simple" crypto has subtle attack vectors; libraries handle them.
2. Hibernate Interceptor fires on every entity persist/update/delete — you don't need to remember to annotate. It captures the entity state before and after, which is exactly what an audit log wants. The AOP aspect fires on method entry/exit — you have to remember `@AuditedAction`, and you don't get the entity diff cleanly (you have to inspect arguments). Hibernate Interceptor is the right tool for "audit every DB change"; AOP is the right tool for "audit every business action" (e.g. "user logged in", which has no entity change). We need both, and we used AOP for both — wrong tool for the entity case.
3. Redis p50 is 0.5ms but p99 is 3ms (network jitter, GC pauses on Redis). 3 round-trips × 3ms = 9ms p99 added to every request. On a 50ms endpoint that's 18% overhead. A single Lua script round-trip is 3ms p99 — 6ms savings. At 1,200 RPS that's a lot of wasted Redis time.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Saying "nothing" — looks like you can't reflect
- Picking something trivial (e.g. "we used the wrong package name")
- Picking something that sounds invented (e.g. "we used MongoDB and regretted it" when you've never used MongoDB)
- Picking crypto (rolling your own crypto is *the* classic mistake — own it honestly)
