### Q14-9: How did you handle disagreements on technical decisions
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Behavioral

**SITUATION:**
The sharpest disagreement: the other backend engineer wanted to split the notification system into a separate microservice immediately (12 months before I believed it was justified); I wanted the modular-monolith path (Q10-2/Q10-3's reasoning). The disagreement was technical, public (a design review), and emotionally loaded — he'd built notification systems at scale before and felt his experience was being discounted; I had the ADR trail arguing our scale didn't justify the ops cost yet.

**TASK:**
Resolve it with the BEST outcome for the product, not the fastest consensus — while keeping the working relationship intact (we pair-reviewed each other's code weekly; a poisoned relationship was a team-level cost).

**ACTION:**
**Step 1 — steelman on record**: I asked him to write the microservice proposal AS the ADR-alternative section (his strongest case, in writing, in the same document as mine — asymmetric effort is where respect shows: I spent MY time making HIS case well). **Step 2 — separate the disagreement's axes**: writing it down revealed we disagreed on FACTS (projected notification volume: he assumed 10× my number based on a pending enterprise deal) and VALUES (ops-complexity tolerance). **Step 3 — resolve facts with evidence**: we got the enterprise deal's real requirements from the PM — 2× volume, not 10× — collapsing one axis entirely. **Step 4 — resolve values with a reversible experiment**: the disagreement shrank to "when" not "if" — we agreed on trigger metrics written INTO the ADR (notification fan-out sustained > 5k/s, or the bulkhead proving insufficient — Q2-14's redesign gets triggered BY DATA, not by either of our opinions) and, as the bridge, he owned the notification module's seam-hardening (the Kafka-shaped event contracts) so his architecture work happened INSIDE the monolith path — his expertise built the extraction readiness, which was genuinely the right work either way. **Step 5 — the relationship repair, deliberately**: we presented the joint ADR together, and I credited the trigger-metric design to him explicitly in the review (because it was his contribution and because credit-where-due is how disagreement stays safe next time).

**RESULT:**
The ADR's trigger metric fired 14 months later — the extraction proceeded on schedule with the seams his work had prepared, and the migration was the cleanest of our extractions. The relationship outcome: we became the pair that senior folks brought contentious designs to, because the team had WATCHED a hard disagreement produce a better process (trigger-metrics-instead-of-opinions) without casualties. The transferable rule I extracted: convert disagreements about the FUTURE into agreements about TRIGGERS — "we'll know it's time when X crosses Y" is a decision two engineers with different priors can both sign.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Steelman-on-record in the shared ADR (asymmetric effort as respect)
- Fact-vs-value decomposition of the disagreement (volume projection resolved with data)
- Trigger-metrics-in-the-ADR (future disagreement → future agreement)
- The bridge role (seam-hardening) using his expertise inside my path
- Joint presentation + explicit credit (relationship maintenance as engineering work)

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. What if the evidence had SUPPORTED his 10× projection?
2. When is a technical disagreement worth escalating past the two of you?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Then we'd have built it — that's what "resolve facts with evidence" means: I wasn't defending my prior, I was defending the EVIDENCE STANDARD, and it binds me symmetrically. With 10× real, the ops-cost argument inverts and his path wins on my own framework. The credibility of trigger-metrics depends entirely on both parties accepting that the metric can go either way; I've also LOST such resolutions and shipped the other design — that history is why the mechanism works.
2. When three conditions hold: the decision is irreversible-ish (a data-model fork), the two parties remain deadlocked after the fact/value decomposition, and the blast radius exceeds our teams (a platform-wide contract). Then it goes to the staff/principal review with BOTH ADRs intact — escalation with the disagreement's structure preserved (not a political summary), because the decider needs the axes, not just the heat. In 9 months, we escalated exactly once — a schema-tenancy decision — and the discipline of the written ADRs made that escalation take one meeting.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Winning-by-seniority stories (title as the resolution mechanism)
- No record of the OTHER side's best case (the ADR asymmetry test)
- Resolution without a relationship plan (the weekly pairing continued — mention it)

---

### Q14-10: What would you add to this project given more time (and what would you NOT)
**DIFFICULTY:** Medium
**CATEGORY TAG:** Behavioral

**SITUATION:**
The interview version of this question is a trap: listing shiny things (Kubernetes! Kafka! Microservices!) signals trend-following; the real answer is a PRIORITIZED list where each item pays a named bill, plus the discipline to name what I would deliberately NOT build.

**TASK:**
(As asked in retrospectives and now in interviews:) given a 3-engineer quarter of "free" time, what is the highest-leverage build list — and what's explicitly out?

**ACTION:**
**Would build, ranked by bills paid:**
1. **The event backbone graduation (Kafka for the notification/analytics path)** — pays the Q2-14 bill before the volume forces it under duress; the seams exist (his Q14-9 work); this is buy-the-dip infrastructure.
2. **The reporting warehouse maturation** — the analytics today queries replicas; a proper columnar store fed by events pays the "cross-service queries post-extraction" bill (Q10-3) and kills the reporting load on OLTP entirely.
3. **Tenant-level performance regression suite in CI** — the whale-org plan-flip (Q12-5) was found by a customer; the skew-scenario load tests exist monthly; wiring a per-tenant latency-budget check into the PR pipeline (against the sanitized snapshot) makes the next skew bug a BUILD failure. Cheap, compounding.
4. **A customer-facing audit/API-usage portal** — Q4-13/Q9-9's dashboards exist internally; exposing usage, audit, and key management to customers converts support tickets into self-service (measured: 30% of our support volume is "what did your system do").
5. **Disaster-recovery game-day automation** — the DR drills (Q6-9) are semi-manual; scripting them (restore-verify as a scheduled job with pass/fail pages) turns a twice-a-year exercise into a continuous guarantee.

**Would NOT build, and why — the discipline half:** microservices beyond the extraction scorecard (the Q10-3 line stands — no service count as a goal); an in-house email delivery engine (provider economics and deliverability expertise favor the vendor — our EmailPort keeps it swappable); multi-region active-active (our RPO/RTO math says single-region + solid DR covers the contract tier we sell — active-active doubles consistency complexity for an SLA we don't charge for); and a plugin marketplace (the extension surface is a security/compatibility commitment that outguns our current team — the API + webhooks ARE the extension story until customers push for more).

**RESULT:**
(Framed as: this is the roadmap I'd defend with any CTO.) The ranked list maps 1:1 to bills ALREADY being paid in incident-hours and support-load — every item's ROI is a number we've measured, not a trend; and the NOT-list is what makes the list credible: constraint is the strategy. In the actual project, item 3 shipped (the CI skew check) and item 1 is in progress — the rest live in the register (Q14-6) with interest-rate scoring, which is exactly where "given more time" answers should live: not in interviews, in a maintained instrument.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Every "yes" pays a NAMED bill (incident-hours, support-load %, churn risk)
- The NOT-list as the credibility half (no-K8s-for-its-own-sake, no in-house email engine)
- Prioritization instrument: the debt/roadmap register with interest rates (Q14-6 continuity)
- Item 3 shipped, item 1 in progress — answers with receipts, not wishes
- Constraint-as-strategy framing for the "more time" question

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. The CEO says "build the plugin marketplace, it's strategy." Now what?
2. Which of your "no" items would flip FIRST, and on what evidence?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Same machinery as Q14-9: decompose the ask into the bill it pays (which customers, what revenue, what retention) and the costs (the security/compatibility commitment in engineer-quarters — I'd scope the v0 honestly: a webhook-templating layer is 80% of the marketplace's actual value at 20% of the commitment, and I'd propose THAT as the strategy-compatible v0). Strategy conversations with engineers who bring scoped options instead of resistance end well; the refusal-reflex is how engineers lose seats at strategy tables.
2. Multi-region flips first: on evidence of (a) an enterprise tier sold with a region-failover SLA, or (b) measured revenue concentration in a geography where latency is costing conversion (the funnel data can show this). Both are NUMBERS; the item moves from my NOT-list to the register the day either lands. The meta-point: "no" is dated — every item on the NOT-list carries its flip condition, which is what makes the discipline engineering instead of stubbornness.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Trend-driven wish lists (K8s/Kafka/GraphQL with no bill attached)
- No NOT-list (undisciplined ambition is a junior signal)
- Nothing SHIPPED from previous "more time" asks (the receipts test)

# End Matter — Cheat Sheet, Common Mistakes, Questions to Ask, Handling Unknown Features
## APPENDIX B — API Logic Deep-Dives (the "walk me through the code" answers)

> The single most common senior-level drill: *"Walk me through what happens, end to end, when this endpoint is called — Controller to database row."* These six walk-throughs cover the APIs interviewers will pick. Rehearse them until you can narrate WITHOUT notes: filter chain → controller → validation → service → transaction boundary → SQL → events → response. The code sketches are the level of detail expected on a whiteboard.

### B.1 — `POST /api/auth/otp/verify` (the security-critical path)

```java
// Filter chain: corsFilter -> RateLimitFilter (per-IP bucket) -> JwtAuthenticationFilter (skipped: public path)
// -> Controller
@PostMapping("/api/auth/otp/verify")
public ResponseEntity<AuthResponse> verify(@Valid @RequestBody OtpVerifyRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(authService.verifyOtp(req.email(), req.otp(), clientMeta()));
}

// Service (transactional)
@Transactional
public AuthResponse verifyOtp(String email, String otp, ClientMeta meta) {
    UserAccount user = userRepository.findByEmail(email)
        .orElseThrow(new BadCredentialsException("INVALID_CREDENTIALS")); // generic: no existence oracle
    // 1. Lockout check (Redis atomic counter, Q4-11)
    if (lockService.isLocked(email)) throw new AccountLockedException(); // 423, generic message
    // 2. Attempt guard: INCR otp:attempts:{hash} -- Lua atomic, TTL 15min
    lockService.recordAttempt(email);
    // 3. Constant-time verify against HASHED otp (BCrypt), expiry via stored expiry column
    if (!otpHasher.matches(otp, user.getOtpHash()) || clock.now().isAfter(user.getOtpExpiry()))
        throw new BadCredentialsException("INVALID_CREDENTIALS");        // 5th failure -> 15min lock
    lockService.clearAttempts(email);
    // 4. Issue tokens: 15-min access JWT (kid, jti) + opaque refresh (SHA-256 hashed into user_session,
    //    family_id for rotation/reuse detection, device fingerprint recorded)
    TokenPair pair = tokenService.issue(user, meta);
    auditService.event("AUTH.OTP_SUCCESS", user);                        // AFTER_COMMIT async write
    return new AuthResponse(pair.accessToken(), pair.refreshCookie());
}
```

**Narration script:** rate-limit layer (per-IP 10/10min) → validation → user lookup with GENERIC error (no oracle) → Redis lockout check → atomic attempt increment → constant-time hash match + expiry → token issuance with hashed refresh + session row → audit event after commit. **Probe next:** "Where exactly can this race?" (two parallel verifies on the 5th attempt — the Lua INCR closes it), "Why hash the OTP in DB?" (dump = inert), "What leaks if you return different errors for unknown email vs wrong OTP?" (existence oracle).

### B.2 — `GET /api/leads?status=HOT&sort=created_at&cursor=...` (the hot read path)

```java
@GetMapping("/api/leads")
public LeadPageResponse list(@Valid LeadFilterRequest filter, @RequestParam Optional<String> cursor) {
    return leadQueryService.list(filter, cursor, securityContext.orgId()); // orgId from JWT claims
}

// Service: NO @Transactional(readOnly=true) needed on primary-routed single query; replica-routed variant has it
public LeadPageResponse list(LeadFilterRequest f, Optional<String> cursor, UUID orgId) {
    Cursor cur = cursorCodec.decode(cursor, f.filterHash());   // Base64 tuple+hash; 409 on cross-query swap
    SortKey sort = sortRegistry.resolve(f.sort());             // allow-list: created_at -> (created_at DESC, id DESC)
    var spec = LeadSpecs.forOrg(orgId)                         // tenant filter FIRST (Q4-6 defense in depth)
        .and(LeadSpecs.status(f.status()))
        .and(LeadSpecs.notDeleted());                          // soft-delete always appended
    if (cur != null) spec.and(LeadSpecs.afterCursor(sort, cur.tuple())); // WHERE (created_at,id) < (:t1,:t2)
    Slice<LeadRow> rows = leadRepository.findBy(spec, PageRequest.ofSize(Math.min(f.limit(), 100)), LeadRow.class);
    return assembler.toResponse(rows, cursorCodec.encodeNext(rows, sort, f.filterHash())); // no total count
}
```

**SQL produced:** `SELECT id, business_name, stage, ... FROM lead WHERE org_id = ? AND status = ? AND deleted_at IS NULL AND (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 51` — index `(org_id, status, created_at DESC, id DESC)` partial `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` → index-only scan with INCLUDE columns. **Probe next:** "Why LIMIT 51?" (fetch one extra row → has_more without COUNT), "Why is `id` in the tuple?" (unique tiebreaker, Q8-3), "What if a filter changes mid-scroll?" (filter-hash → 409 CURSOR_MISMATCH).

### B.3 — `POST /api/outreach/generate` (the metered AI path)

```java
@PostMapping("/api/outreach/generate")
public ResponseEntity<GenerationResponse> generate(@Valid @RequestBody GenerateRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.accepted().body(outreachFacade.generate(req.leadId(), securityContext.principal()));
}

// Facade — the 6-step flow (Q3-20's Facade pattern)
@Transactional
public GenerationResponse generate(UUID leadId, Principal p) {
    Lead lead = leadRepository.findInOrg(leadId, p.orgId()).orElseThrow(LeadNotFoundException::new); // 404 cross-tenant
    int cost = creditCosts.of("AI_GENERATION");                       // Redis-cached config, Q7-2
    creditService.reserve(p.userId(), cost, "AI_GEN", key(leadId));   // conditional UPDATE + PENDING ledger row
    try {
        GeneratedEmail email = aiGateway.generate(promptManager.build(lead, p.orgTone()), timeout(20s));
        // aiGateway: breaker + retry(429/5xx) + fallback-to-template chain (Q3-12); fallback marks AI_FALLBACK,
        // refunds the reservation, returns within budget -- user never sees a 500 for provider downtime
        validator.assertSafe(email);                                  // schema + injection-marker guards
        Generation gen = generationRepository.save(Generation.of(lead, email));
        creditService.confirm(key(leadId));                           // PENDING -> POSTED
        eventPublisher.publishEvent(new OutreachGeneratedEvent(gen.id(), p.orgId()));
        return GenerationResponse.of(gen);
    } catch (AiValidationException e) {
        creditService.refund(key(leadId));                            // compensating ledger entry
        throw e;
    }
}
// Event listeners (AFTER_COMMIT + @Async): analytics counter, hot-lead re-score, websocket push to UI
```

**Narration script:** tenant-scoped fetch (404 not 403) → credit RESERVATION (conditional UPDATE — the row is the lock) → provider call OUTSIDE the lock via the gateway's breaker stack → validation → confirm reservation → AFTER_COMMIT side effects. **Probe next:** "Crash after reserve, before confirm?" (sweeper reaps PENDING > 5 min — refund; idempotency key makes the retry safe), "Why not deduct AFTER the AI call?" (double-spend window), "What does the user see when the breaker is open?" (template fallback + AI_FALLBACK tag + no charge).

### B.4 — `POST /api/webhooks/stripe` (the money path)

```java
@PostMapping(value = "/api/webhooks/stripe", consumes = "application/json")
public ResponseEntity<Void> onStripe(HttpServletRequest request) throws IOException {
    String raw = request.getInputStream().readAllBytes()...;        // RAW body: signature needs exact bytes
    Event event = stripeVerifier.verifyAndParse(raw, sigHeader, tolerance(300s)); // HMAC + timestamp window
    webhookIngest.ingest(Provider.STRIPE, event.id(), event.type(), raw); // persist-then-ack
    return ResponseEntity.ok().build();                             // 2xx AFTER durability, NOT after processing
}

// Ingest: INSERT webhook_event (provider, event_id UNIQUE, payload, status=RECEIVED) -- dedupe is structural.
// Async worker (job-table, SKIP LOCKED):
@Transactional
public void process(WebhookEvent we) {
    switch (we.type()) {
        case "checkout.session.completed" -> billingService.activateSubscription(we); // idempotent: session id
        case "invoice.payment_failed"     -> billingService.markDunning(we);
        case "customer.subscription.deleted" -> billingService.downgrade(we);
        default -> webhookRegistry.markUnhandled(we);               // 2xx already sent; unknown = data, not error
    }
    we.markProcessed();
}
```

**Narration script:** raw-byte capture → signature + tolerance → persist with UNIQUE event-id (replays no-op structurally) → 2xx immediately → async idempotent handlers keyed on provider object ids → freshness alarm (no webhooks in 30 min = page) + hourly reconciliation sweep (RECEIVED older than 10 min → re-dispatch). **Probe next:** "Why 2xx before processing?" (provider retry storms + duplicate processing otherwise), "Handler crashes mid-activate?" (transaction rolls back, row stays RECEIVED, sweep re-dispatches — handler idempotency absorbs it), "A replayed checkout.completed for an already-active sub?" (idempotency key → no-op, ledger unchanged).

### B.5 — `POST /api/meetings/book` (the distributed-write path)

```java
@Transactional
public BookingResponse book(UUID slotId, BookerIdentity booker) {
    // 1. Atomic slot claim: DB is the concurrency control (Q6-13)
    int claimed = slotRepository.claim(slotId, PROPOSED, BOOKED);   // UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND status='PROPOSED'
    if (claimed == 0) throw new SlotAlreadyBookedException();       // 409 + next-best slots
    MeetingSlot slot = slotRepository.findBooked(slotId);
    // 2. Google write AFTER local commit via outbox -- we do NOT call Google inside the transaction (Q6-11:
    //    no external I/O while holding row locks). Outbox row = instruction; relay executes events.insert.
    outbox.publish(new CalendarEventCreate(slot.id(), slot.window(), booker, slot.organizerToken()));
    eventPublisher.publishEvent(new MeetingBookedEvent(slot.id(), slot.orgId())); // AFTER_COMMIT: ICS emails
    return BookingResponse.confirmed(slot, "PENDING_CALENDAR_SYNC");
}
// Relay worker: executes CalendarCreate via Google API (refresh token envelope-decrypted per use, Q9-9),
// stores google_event_id back on the slot; failure -> compensation job retries -> if Google says CONFLICT,
// slot marked CONFLICT + apology email + re-propose flow (Q2-12's distributed-write failure story).
```

**Narration script:** conditional claim (rows-affected verdict) → outbox instruction → commit → relay does the Google call with compensation semantics → reconciliation on conflict. **Probe next:** "Why not call Google in the transaction?" (lock held across network I/O — the pool-starvation incident class, Q6-13), "Two leads click the same slot?" (second UPDATE matches zero rows → 409), "DB committed but Google insert fails permanently?" (compensation job + CONFLICT state + human-readable recovery — never silently lost).

### B.6 — `POST /api/leads/import` (the batch path)

```java
@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
public ResponseEntity<ImportJobResponse> importLeads(@RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file) {
    validator.assertCsv(file);                       // magic-byte sniff + size cap (413 clean, Q3-15)
    String key = objectStorage.put(file);            // STREAMED to S3 (constant JVM memory), sha256 recorded
    ImportJob job = importService.enqueue(key, file.getSize(), securityContext.orgId()); // job-table row
    return ResponseEntity.accepted().body(ImportJobResponse.of(job));   // 202 + job id -- never parse inline
}
// Spring Batch job: FlatFileItemReader (from S3 stream, fetchSize=chunk) -> validate/transform processor
// (schema, dupes-in-file, dedupe-against-db via idempotency hash) -> JPA batch writer (jdbc batch_size 50,
// SEQUENCE ids, clear() per chunk 100 -- Q5-16's full stack). Progress = first-class resource:
// GET /api/leads/import/{jobId} -> {processed: 240000, total: 500000, rejected: 1204, reportUrl: ...}
```

**Narration script:** sniff + stream-to-storage (never heap) → 202 immediately → chunked batch with per-chunk commit checkpoints (crash = resume from last chunk, Q5-16) → per-row errors collected to a downloadable report → progress endpoint polled/SSE'd. **Probe next:** "Why not parse in the request?" (timeout lottery + deploy hazard, Q11-7), "Duplicate rows in the file AND in DB?" (idempotency hash per row + UNIQUE constraint — rejected-with-report, not silently merged), "A 2GB file?" (presigned direct-to-storage protocol, Q8-7 — the app never touches bytes).

## Common Mistakes to Avoid in the Interview

1. **Mentioning Next.js / Node / npm / Prisma as the backend** — instant fail. The story is **Java Spring Boot + Hibernate + PostgreSQL + Redis**. Frontend (React + TypeScript) may be mentioned but only as a client.

2. **Saying "we use microservices"** for a monolith — looks like you don't know your own architecture.

3. **Saying "100% test coverage"** — interviewers know this is impossible without writing useless tests. Say 78% line, 64% branch (and explain why you don't enforce 100%).

4. **Saying "p99 = 50ms"** — sounds like you're not measuring. Real p99 for a CRUD app with DB + Redis + external APIs is 200-1000ms. We say p99 = 540ms.

5. **Saying "we use Kafka" when you actually use Spring Events** — be honest. We use both, with Kafka only for the few events that will cross a service boundary.

6. **Saying "no production incidents"** — looks fake. We had a 23-minute outage in March 2026 (Hibernate config). Own it.

7. **Saying "I built everything"** — bus factor 1 is bad. We say 70% ownership + 2 backend engineers + clear context boundaries.

8. **Quoting fake scale numbers** — be ready to defend every number. "3,200 paying orgs" is defensible; "1 million users" sounds invented.

9. **Skipping the "why" for tech choices** — interviewers want the *reasoning*, not the choice. "Postgres because JSONB + CTE" beats "Postgres because everyone uses it".

10. **Forgetting operational + observability** — a senior engineer owns the deploy + monitoring + on-call. Saying "the devops team handles it" is a junior answer.

11. **Not knowing your `application.yml`** — if asked "what's in your HikariCP config" and you don't know, you don't own the codebase. Know the key configs (pool size, connection timeout, leak detection).

12. **Treating testing as an afterthought** — seniors have a testing strategy. Unit + slice + integration + E2E + contract + performance + chaos. Saying "we write unit tests" is not a strategy.

13. **Not knowing the failure modes** — every senior knows what happens when Redis is down, when Stripe is down, when the DB primary fails. Saying "we have backups" doesn't answer the question.

14. **Overusing "AI" without specifics** — say which model, what prompt, what cost, what cache hit ratio. "We use AI for outreach" is a junior answer.

15. **Skipping cost** — LLM is real money ($4,200/month for us). Stripe is real money (2.9% + ₹3 per transaction). Saying "we don't track cost" is a fail.

16. **Saying "we use Spring Data JPA" without knowing N+1** — N+1 is the #1 Hibernate interview question. If you don't know `@EntityGraph`, you don't know Hibernate.

17. **Saying `EAGER` is fine** — EAGER on `@ManyToOne` is the N+1 trap. Always override to `LAZY`.

18. **Saying "we use REST" without specifics** — every backend uses REST. Drill on idempotency, status codes (202 vs 201), pagination (cursor vs offset), rate limiting, versioning.

19. **Not knowing your Stripe webhook verification** — raw bytes (not JSON-parsed first), `Webhook.constructEvent`, idempotency via `event_id`. This is a standard interview question.

20. **Saying "we use Docker" without the Dockerfile** — a senior can sketch a multi-stage Dockerfile with Spring Boot layered jar + Eclipse Temurin base.

## Questions to Ask the Interviewer About Their System

Ask these *after* they've asked their questions. Interviewers at Uber/Meta/NetApp will judge you on the quality of your questions — bad questions signal lack of curiosity.

### About their architecture
- "Walk me through your service architecture. Are you a monolith, microservices, or hybrid?"
- "What's your primary datastore? Why did you choose it?"
- "How do you handle cross-service communication — sync REST, events, both?"
- "What's your largest table, and how is it partitioned?"
- "How do you handle multi-tenancy — schema-per-tenant, shared schema with `tenant_id`, or row-level security?"

### About their scale + performance
- "What's your peak RPS? p95 latency? uptime SLA?"
- "What's the biggest performance bottleneck you're working on right now?"
- "How do you handle a slow external API call — circuit breaker, timeout, both?"
- "What's your cache hit ratio target, and what do you do when it drops?"
- "How do you size your connection pools? Database? Redis?"

### About their team + process
- "How is the backend team organised — by service, by feature, by layer?"
- "What does your on-call rotation look like? What's the alert volume?"
- "What's your deploy frequency? Lead time? MTTR?"
- "How do you handle tech debt — dedicated time, embedded in sprints, neither?"
- "What's your code review process? Who approves PRs?"

### About their tech + tools
- "What version of Java + Spring Boot are you on? Any upgrade plans?"
- "How do you manage secrets — Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, something else?"
- "What's your observability stack — Prometheus, Datadog, something else?"
- "How do you test — what's your pyramid? Do you have chaos testing?"
- "What's your CI/CD pipeline — Jenkins, GitHub Actions, something else?"

### About their business
- "What's the ICP for your product? What's the biggest customer pain point right now?"
- "How do you measure success — what's your north-star metric?"
- "What's the next big feature on your roadmap?"
- "What's the biggest risk to the business right now?"
- "How does this team's work tie to revenue?"

### About the role + you
- "What does success look like in this role in the first 6 months?"
- "What's the biggest challenge the person in this role will face?"
- "What's the team's technical direction for the next year?"
- "How do you support learning — conferences, books, internal talks?"
- "What's the path to senior/staff engineer at your company?"

### Smart follow-ups
- After they answer "we use Kafka": "What's your consumer lag monitoring? How do you handle a backlog?"
- After they answer "we use microservices": "How do you handle distributed transactions? Sagas, 2PC, eventual consistency?"
- After they answer "we have 99.99% uptime": "What's your largest outage in the last year? What did you learn?"
- After they answer "we use Postgres": "Have you hit any partitioning limits? How do you handle a 1TB+ table?"
- After they answer "we use Spring Boot": "Are you on 3.x? Have you tried virtual threads?"

---

## How to Handle Questions About Features You Did Not Build

You will be asked about features you don't know. The interviewer knows you didn't build everything. The right answer is **honest + engaged**, not "I don't know."

### Pattern: Honest + show curiosity + pivot to what you know

**Wrong:** "I don't know, I didn't work on that." → Looks like you have no curiosity.

**Better:** "I didn't personally build that — my colleague owned the meeting/calendar module. From talking to him, the design was: [sketch what you know]. I'd want to learn more — what aspect are you most curious about?"

**Pattern: Show your reasoning even without the specific knowledge**

**Wrong:** "We use GraphQL. I don't know the schema." → Looks like you don't understand your own stack.

**Better:** "We use REST today. We considered GraphQL but didn't adopt because: (a) our frontend is our own SPA, so over-fetching isn't a problem; (b) GraphQL adds schema management complexity; (c) our clients are mostly internal (we don't have third-party API consumers). If we were building a public API for third parties, GraphQL would be more attractive."

### Pattern: "I haven't worked with X, but here's how I'd approach it"

For unfamiliar tech (Kafka Streams, Cassandra, gRPC, CockroachDB), say: "I haven't worked with Cassandra, but my understanding is it's good for write-heavy workloads with eventual consistency. If I needed it for a feature, I'd read the docs + talk to someone who's used it + spike a small prototype in a week."

### Pattern: When you genuinely don't know — ask back

If asked "what's the JVM flag for X" and you don't know: "I don't remember the exact flag — let me think about how I'd find it. I'd check `java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep <keyword>` to list JVM flags, or read the OpenJDK docs, or check our `Dockerfile` for the flags we set. Our current JVM args are `-Xmx2g -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:+UseStringDeduplication` — I don't remember the exact flag for X, but I'd find it in 5 minutes."

### Pattern: When the question is unfair (a library you've never used)

"We don't use RxJava — we use Project Reactor via WebClient. They're similar reactive libraries. I haven't used RxJava specifically, but the concepts (observables, backpressure, schedulers) translate. If you want me to compare them, I can tell you what I know about Reactor."

### Pattern: When the question is about a feature you've used but not built

"I use Kafka as a producer + consumer but I didn't set up our Kafka cluster — our devops contractor did. From talking to him, our cluster is 3 brokers, replication factor 3, retention 7 days. I know how to publish + consume + handle consumer lag, but I haven't done the broker-level admin (reassigning partitions, balancing leadership)."

### Pattern: When the question is genuinely hard + you don't know — don't fake it

If asked "design Twitter's timeline at scale" and you've never thought about it: "I haven't designed a system at Twitter's scale. Let me try: I'd start with the read-heavy nature — most timelines are reads. The fan-out approach: on tweet write, write to the tweet DB + push to followers' timeline caches (Redis sorted sets). The challenge is the celebrity fan-out — a celebrity with 100M followers can't push to 100M caches on each tweet. Hybrid: pull for celebrity timelines, push for normal users. I'd want to validate this against Twitter's engineering blog posts before committing."

### Summary
1. **Don't fake knowledge** — interviewers at Uber/Meta have heard every evasive answer.
2. **Show curiosity** — you don't have to know everything; you have to want to learn.
3. **Pivot to what you know** — bridge to a related topic.
4. **Quantify when you don't know** — "I haven't done X, but here's how I'd approach it in a week."

---

## CATEGORY 15 — BONUS: ADVANCED & TWISTED QUESTIONS (Uber / Meta / Amazon Drill-Downs)

> **Purpose of this appendix.** The 14 categories above are the *base reference*. The questions below are the **twisted, end-to-end, "what if the world breaks"** variants that Uber / Meta / Amazon interviewers use to separate mid-level from senior. Every question here includes (where relevant) a Java/Spring Boot code snippet, a logic trace, an ASCII diagram, or a DB schema. Treat these as the final stretch before your interview.

### Q-Bonus-1: A user double-clicks "Generate Outreach" 10 times in 800ms. Your credit-deduction service must deduct exactly 50 credits once, not 500. Walk me through the entire defence, end to end, with code.
- **Difficulty:** Expert
- **Category:** System Design / Concurrency / Spring Boot
- **Tags:** idempotency, pessimistic-lock, credit-ledger, double-spend

**ANSWER:**
The defence is layered — a client-supplied **idempotency key**, a **DB unique constraint** on it, a **pessimistic row lock** on the credit balance, and an **append-only credit ledger** so the deduction is auditable and replayable. The idempotency key is the first line: the frontend generates a UUID per "Generate Outreach" button arming and sends it in the `Idempotency-Key` header. The `OutreachController` forwards it to `CreditService.deduct(userId, amount, idempotencyKey)`, which is `@Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW)` so the deduction commits independently of the (longer) outreach-generation transaction.

Inside `deduct`, the service first tries `INSERT INTO credit_ledger (user_id, delta, idempotency_key, ...) VALUES (..., -50, ?)`; a unique index on `(user_id, idempotency_key)` makes the second click's insert throw a `DataIntegrityViolationException`, which we catch and translate into a no-op return of the first call's result. We also `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` the `credit_balance` row to prevent two concurrent first-clicks from both reading 50 and both writing 0 — the lock serialises them, and the one that wins the insert commits, the other rolls back to the unique violation. The ledger row is the source of truth; the `credit_balance` row is a **materialised view** that we keep in sync with `@Transactional` write of both rows in one transaction.

**Code:**
```java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CreditService {
  private final CreditLedgerRepository ledgerRepo;
  private final CreditBalanceRepository balanceRepo;   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE

  @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW, isolation = REPEATABLE_READ)
  public DeductResult deduct(UUID userId, int amount, String idempotencyKey) {
    // 1. Idempotency: insert into ledger first; unique index rejects dupes.
    try {
      ledgerRepo.insert(new CreditLedgerRow(userId, -amount, idempotencyKey, "OUTREACH", now()));
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException dup) {
      // Second click — return the cached result of the first.
      return ledgerRepo.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey).result();
    }
    // 2. Pessimistic lock on balance; re-check sufficiency under lock.
    CreditBalance bal = balanceRepo.findAndLockByUserId(userId);   // SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
    if (bal.getBalance() < amount) throw new InsufficientCreditsException(userId, amount);
    bal.setBalance(bal.getBalance() - amount);
    balanceRepo.save(bal);                                  // UPDATE credit_balance
    auditPublisher.publish(new CreditsDeducted(userId, amount, idempotencyKey));
    return new DeductResult(bal.getBalance(), idempotencyKey);
  }
}
```

**End-to-end trace:** `POST /api/leads/{id}/outreach` → `Idempotency-Key` header → `OutreachController.generate()` validates `@Valid GenerateOutreachRequest` → calls `CreditService.deduct()` (new tx, locks row, inserts ledger, updates balance, publishes `CreditsDeducted` via `ApplicationEventPublisher`) → on success calls `AiOutreachService.generate()` (separate tx, calls LLM via `WebClient` + Resilience4j circuit breaker, persists `messages` rows) → returns variants. Second click: controller sees same `Idempotency-Key`, `CreditService.deduct()` hits unique-index violation, returns cached result, AI service is never called, user sees the first response. If AI service fails after deduction, the `CreditsDeducted` event triggers a compensating `CreditService.refund()` that writes a `+50` ledger row under the **same idempotency key (suffixed `-refund`)** — no double refund.

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- `Idempotency-Key` header (client-generated UUID)
- `@Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW)` so deduction commits before the slow LLM call
- Unique index on `(user_id, idempotency_key)` as the concurrency primitive
- `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (pessimistic lock) on `credit_balance`
- Append-only `credit_ledger` (event-sourcing style), balance = materialised projection
- `DataIntegrityViolationException` → no-op (return cached result)
- Compensating refund on downstream failure, idempotency key suffixed

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` if you already have the unique index on idempotency key?
2. What if the user legitimately wants to generate outreach twice (two different emails)?
3. The refund path: how do you make sure the refund itself is idempotent if the compensation event is delivered twice?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. The unique index protects the *ledger insert* (prevents two +50 deductions). It does not protect the *balance read-modify-write* between two *different* idempotency keys that race on the same user (e.g., the user opens two tabs and clicks Generate with two different keys — both would pass the unique check but both would read balance=50 and write 0, losing 50 credits). `FOR UPDATE` serialises the balance access across *all* deductions regardless of idempotency key. The unique index handles duplicate-clicks; the pessimistic lock handles concurrent-but-distinct operations.
2. Each legitimate generation gets a fresh `Idempotency-Key` from the frontend (a new button arming). The ledger has many rows for the same user, each with a distinct key. The balance decreases by the sum. The idempotency key protects *this exact operation*, not "this user can only ever buy once."
3. The refund ledger row carries its own idempotency key = `{originalKey}-refund`. A unique index on `(user_id, idempotency_key)` means a second delivery of the refund event hits the same unique violation and no-ops. The consumer that publishes the compensation is itself at-least-once; the ledger's uniqueness makes it effectively-once.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- "We use Redis `SETNX` on the idempotency key" — Redis is volatile; a crash between Redis-set and DB-write loses the guarantee. The DB unique index is the durable primitive.
- "We check `if (balance >= amount)` then update" without a lock — classic TOCTOU race; two threads both pass the check, both deduct, balance goes negative.
- Putting the deduction in the same transaction as the LLM call — if the LLM times out (30s) the credit row is locked for 30s, throughput collapses.

### Q-Bonus-2: The Stripe webhook for `checkout.session.completed` arrives BEFORE your own `POST /api/payments/create-checkout-session` handler has committed the `Order` row to the DB. The webhook handler can't find the order. How do you design the fix, with code and a diagram?
- **Difficulty:** Expert
- **Category:** System Design / Distributed Systems / Integrations
- **Tags:** outbox, eventual-consistency, webhook, race-condition, dual-write

**ANSWER:**
This is the classic **dual-write race**: two independent systems (Stripe and our DB) commit in nondeterministic order. The fix is the **transactional outbox pattern** — the `Order` row and a `pending_webhook` expectation are written in the *same* DB transaction, so by the time Stripe can fire a webhook, the order is durable. But that doesn't fully solve it: Stripe can still deliver the webhook before the local transaction commits if the redirect and the webhook race. So the webhook handler must **retry with backoff** when the order isn't found, and the checkout-session handler must **publish an `OrderCommitted` event** that the webhook handler can wait on.

Concretely: `create-checkout-session` writes `Order(status=PENDING)` + `CheckoutSession(stripeSessionId)` in one `@Transactional` block, then redirects to Stripe. Stripe redirects the user's browser back to us (fast) AND POSTs the webhook (separate request). If the webhook arrives during the 50ms commit window, it sees no order → it must return `202 Accepted` (NOT 500, otherwise Stripe retries immediately and may DDoS us) and rely on Stripe's own retry schedule (which has exponential backoff). On the next Stripe retry (minutes later), the order is committed and processing succeeds. For faster recovery, the webhook handler can also enqueue a delayed "reconcile this session" job onto a Redis sorted set, polled by a worker that retries once the order appears.

**Diagram (race window + fix):**
```
 T0  create-checkout-session: BEGIN TX
       INSERT orders (id=O1, status=PENDING)
       INSERT checkout_sessions (order=O1, stripe=cs_test_123)
       COMMIT                          <-- durable point
 T1  redirect user → Stripe
 T2  user pays on Stripe
 T3  Stripe redirects browser → /success?session=cs_test_123   (may arrive BEFORE T0 commit!)
 T4  Stripe POSTs webhook → /webhooks/stripe (event=checkout.session.completed)
       └─ handler: SELECT order WHERE stripe_session_id=cs_test_123
            ├─ found? process: mark PAID, grant credits, publish OrderPaid
            └─ not found? return 202; enqueue delayed reconcile(cs_test_123, runAt=now+10s)
 T5  Reconcile worker pops delayed job: SELECT order ... ; if still missing, retry up to 5 min
```

**Code (webhook handler with retry-on-missing):**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/webhooks/stripe")
public class StripeWebhookController {
  private final OrderService orderService;
  private final StripeWebhookVerifier verifier;   // raw body + signature
  private final ReconcileQueue reconcileQueue;

  @PostMapping(consumes = "application/json")
  public ResponseEntity<Void> handle(@RequestBody byte[] rawBody,
                                     @RequestHeader("Stripe-Signature") String sig) {
    Event event = verifier.verify(rawBody, sig);   // throws → 400 (Stripe won't retry on 400)
    if (event.getType().equals("checkout.session.completed")) {
      String stripeSessionId = ((Session) event.getDataObjectDeserializer().getObject().get()).getId();
      try {
        orderService.markPaid(stripeSessionId, event.getId());   // idempotent on event.getId()
      } catch (OrderNotFoundException missing) {
        // Race: webhook beat the commit. Accept; Stripe will retry. Also schedule our own retry.
        reconcileQueue.enqueue(stripeSessionId, Duration.ofSeconds(10));
      }
      return ResponseEntity.accepted().build();    // 202 — Stripe counts as delivered
    }
    return ResponseEntity.ok().build();
  }
}
```

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Transactional outbox (write order + session in one tx)
- 202 Accepted (not 500) on missing-order so Stripe retries with backoff, not a storm
- Stripe webhook signature verification on **raw bytes** (not parsed JSON)
- Idempotency on `event.getId()` (Stripe may deliver the same event twice)
- Delayed reconcile queue (Redis ZSET `score=runAt`) as a hedge against Stripe dropping retries
- `OrderNotFoundException` is a *transient* error in this race, not a 500

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Stripe guarantees at-least-once delivery. How do you make `markPaid` idempotent?
2. What if the user's browser redirect to `/success` arrives before the webhook AND before the commit?
3. Why not just put the webhook processing in a queue and always return 202?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. `markPaid(stripeSessionId, eventId)` first inserts into `processed_webhook_events(event_id)` under a unique index; on duplicate it no-ops. Then it transitions the order `PENDING → PAID` with an `UPDATE orders SET status='PAID' WHERE id=? AND status='PENDING'` (optimistic conditional update — only one call wins). Credits are granted in the same transaction via the credit ledger with idempotency key = `event_id`.
2. The `/success` page is a *status-polling* page, not a *processing* page. It calls `GET /api/payments/verify-session?session=cs_test_123`, which returns the order's current status. If still PENDING (webhook hasn't landed), the frontend polls every 2s for up to 30s. The page never *processes* payment based on the redirect — only the webhook does. This prevents the redirect from being a second source of truth.
3. You can, and many teams do — it simplifies the handler to "verify signature → enqueue → 202". The trade-off is latency: the user's `/success` page must wait for the queue worker to process, which adds p99 latency. We chose to process synchronously when possible (fast path) and fall back to the queue only on the race window. This keeps p99 payment-confirmation latency under 2s for the 99.9% of webhooks that arrive after commit.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Returning 500 when the order is missing — Stripe will retry *immediately* and aggressively, multiplying load during the race window.
- Verifying the signature on parsed JSON — `Stripe.Webhook.constructEvent` needs the raw body; a JSON re-serialise changes key ordering and breaks the signature.
- Processing the payment in the `/success` redirect handler — that's a duplicate-processing source and ignores the webhook entirely.

### Q-Bonus-3: Redis goes down during a rate-limit check on `/api/auth/otp/request`. Do you fail open (allow the request) or fail closed (deny it)? Justify with code and the security tradeoff.
- **Difficulty:** Hard
- **Category:** Spring Security / Redis / Resilience
- **Tags:** fail-open, fail-closed, rate-limit, resilience4j, graceful-degradation

**ANSWER:**
The answer depends on the endpoint's risk profile. For **public, brute-forceable, high-blast-radius** endpoints (OTP request, magic-link request, login), you **fail closed** — a Redis outage must not turn your rate limiter into an open door, because an attacker can now fire unlimited OTPs, triggering SMS/email cost and user harassment. For **low-risk, already-authenticated** endpoints (e.g., listing leads), you **fail open** — denying a logged-in user because Redis hiccupped is a worse UX than a temporary over-allow.

In AcquisitionOS, the `RateLimitAspect` (Spring AOP) wraps auth endpoints with a Resilience4j `CircuitBreaker` around the Redis call. When the circuit opens (Redis down), the aspect checks the `@RateLimit(failOpen=false)` annotation. For OTP, `failOpen=false` → it throws `RateLimitServiceUnavailable` → mapped to `503` with a `Retry-After: 30` header. For lead-listing, `failOpen=true` → it logs a warning, increments a local in-memory counter (best-effort), and lets the request through. We also keep a **local fallback limiter** (Caffeine, per-instance, per-IP) so even when Redis is down we have *some* protection on auth endpoints — it can't stop cross-instance attacks, but it stops a single instance from being a firehose.

**Code:**
```java
@Aspect
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class RateLimitAspect {
  private final RedisRateLimiter redisLimiter;
  private final LocalRateLimiter localLimiter;   // Caffeine fallback
  private final CircuitBreaker redisCb;          // Resilience4j

  @Around("@annotation(rateLimit)")
  public Object around(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, RateLimit rateLimit) throws Throwable {
    String key = buildKey(pjp, rateLimit);
    boolean allowed;
    try {
      allowed = redisCb.executeSupplier(() -> redisLimiter.allow(key, rateLimit.limit(), rateLimit.window()));
    } catch (CallNotPermittedException cbOpen) {
      // Redis is down. Decision time.
      if (rateLimit.failOpen()) {
        allowed = localLimiter.allow(key, rateLimit.limit() / 2, rateLimit.window()); // half the rate locally
        log.warn("Redis rate-limit down; failing OPEN with local cap for key={}", key);
      } else {
        log.error("Redis rate-limit down; failing CLOSED for protected key={}", key);
        throw new RateLimitServiceUnavailableException(rateLimit.window());
      }
    }
    if (!allowed) throw new TooManyRequestsException(rateLimit.window());
    return pjp.proceed();
  }
}

// Usage:
@PostMapping("/auth/otp/request")
@RateLimit(limit = 5, window = 900, failOpen = false)   // 5 per 15 min, fail CLOSED
public void requestOtp(@Valid @RequestBody OtpRequest req) { ... }

@GetMapping("/leads")
@RateLimit(limit = 100, window = 60, failOpen = true)   // 100 per min, fail OPEN
public Page<Lead> listLeads(@Valid Pageable pageable) { ... }
```

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Fail-open vs fail-closed as a per-endpoint decision (risk-based)
- Resilience4j `CircuitBreaker` around the Redis call
- Local fallback (Caffeine) halves the rate when Redis is down — degrades, doesn't collapse
- `503` + `Retry-After` for fail-closed; structured log for fail-open
- Annotation-driven (`@RateLimit(failOpen=...)`) so the decision lives with the endpoint

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. The local Caffeine limiter is per-instance. An attacker rotates across your 4 ECS tasks — each sees 1/4 of the traffic. How do you still protect?
2. Why a circuit breaker and not just a try-catch?
3. How long is the circuit open? What's the half-open behaviour?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. With 4 instances each allowing `limit/2`, an attacker rotating IPs across all 4 gets `4 × limit/2 = 2×limit` — still capped, not unlimited. The fallback is a *degradation*, not a full bypass. If Redis is down for long, we alert ops and can manually switch auth endpoints to a hard 429-everything via a feature flag. The deeper fix is a Redis cluster (3 shards + replicas) so a single-node outage doesn't take the limiter down — we have that in prod, this is the "cluster is down" worst case.
2. A try-catch would hit Redis on every request even when it's down, adding 200ms of connection-timeout per request and serving no purpose. The circuit breaker trips after N failures, stops calling Redis, and fails fast (1ms) — it protects both the request latency and the Redis instance from thundering-herd reconnects.
3. `slidingWindowType=COUNT_BASED, slidingWindowSize=20, failureRateThreshold=50%, waitDurationInOpenState=30s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState=3`. After 30s open, it lets 3 probe calls through; if they succeed, the circuit closes; if they fail, it re-opens for another 30s. This auto-recovers when Redis comes back without manual intervention.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- "Always fail open" — that turns Redis downtime into an auth-bypass window.
- "Always fail closed" — that makes Redis a single point of failure for the entire site.
- No circuit breaker, just a try-catch with a connection timeout — every request pays the timeout when Redis is down.

### Q-Bonus-4: Design the database schema for the credit/billing system as an event-sourced ledger. Show tables, indexes, and the balance-projection query.
- **Difficulty:** Hard
- **Category:** Hibernate/JPA / Database Design
- **Tags:** event-sourcing, credit-ledger, materialised-view, append-only

**ANSWER:**
The credit system is modelled as an **append-only event log** (`credit_ledger`) plus a **materialised balance** (`credit_balance`) kept in sync by the same transaction. The ledger is the source of truth; the balance is a cache. This gives us: (1) full auditability (every credit change is a row with a reason), (2) replayability (drop the balance table, re-derive from the ledger), (3) idempotency (unique index on idempotency_key), and (4) a clean refund/compensation model (a `+amount` row with a reference to the original `-amount` row).

**Schema:**
```sql
-- Append-only event log. NEVER UPDATE or DELETE a row here.
CREATE TABLE credit_ledger (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id         UUID    NOT NULL,
  org_id          UUID    NOT NULL,
  delta           INTEGER NOT NULL,              -- negative = deduction, positive = grant/refund
  balance_after   INTEGER NOT NULL,              -- snapshot for fast read (denormalised)
  reason          VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,          -- OUTREACH, SIGNUP_BONUS, REFUND, TOPUP, RENEWAL, ADJUSTMENT
  ref_type        VARCHAR(40),                   -- 'order', 'lead', 'message' (polymorphic ref)
  ref_id          UUID,
  idempotency_key VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,         -- client UUID or "{eventId}-refund"
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  created_by      UUID,                          -- admin who adjusted, if reason=ADJUSTMENT
  CONSTRAINT chk_delta_nonzero CHECK (delta <> 0)
);

-- One deduction per (user, idempotency_key). Refunds use a different key.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_ledger_user_idem ON credit_ledger (user_id, idempotency_key);

-- The history is the common query; index it.
CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_user_time ON credit_ledger (user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_ledger_org_reason_time ON credit_ledger (org_id, reason, created_at DESC);

-- Materialised current balance. Updated atomically with each ledger row.
CREATE TABLE credit_balance (
  user_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id),
  org_id         UUID    NOT NULL,
  balance        INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0),
  reserved       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,    -- in-flight (held but not yet deducted)
  updated_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_balance_org ON credit_balance (org_id);

-- Monthly plan grant + renewal tracking
CREATE TABLE subscription (
  id                  UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id              UUID NOT NULL,
  plan                VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,        -- FREE, STARTER, PRO, ELITE
  stripe_customer_id  VARCHAR(64),
  stripe_sub_id       VARCHAR(64),
  status              VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,       -- TRIALING, ACTIVE, PAST_DUE, CANCELED
  monthly_credits     INTEGER NOT NULL,
  current_period_end  TIMESTAMPTZ,
  created_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_sub_org ON subscription (org_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_sub_renewal ON subscription (current_period_end) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Processed Stripe events (webhook idempotency)
CREATE TABLE processed_webhook_events (
  event_id      VARCHAR(80) PRIMARY KEY,
  event_type    VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  processed_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

**Balance projection (re-derive if `credit_balance` is ever lost):**
```sql
-- Idempotent rebuild: for each user, sum deltas in created_at order, carrying the running balance.
WITH running AS (
  SELECT user_id, delta,
         SUM(delta) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at, id) AS balance
  FROM credit_ledger
)
SELECT user_id, MAX(balance) AS current_balance
FROM running
GROUP BY user_id;
-- Then: INSERT INTO credit_balance (user_id, balance) SELECT ... ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE SET balance = EXCLUDED.balance;
```

**JPA mapping (sketch):**
```java
@Entity @Table(name = "credit_ledger")
public class CreditLedgerRow {
  @Id @GeneratedValue Long id;
  private UUID userId; private UUID orgId;
  private int delta; private int balanceAfter;
  @Enumerated(STRING) private CreditReason reason;
  private String refType; private UUID refId;
  @Column(nullable = false) private String idempotencyKey;
  @CreatedDate private Instant createdAt;
  private UUID createdBy;
}

public interface CreditLedgerRepository extends JpaRepository<CreditLedgerRow, Long> {
  @Query("SELECT l FROM CreditLedgerRow l WHERE l.userId = :uid ORDER BY l.createdAt DESC")
  List<CreditLedgerRow> history(UUID uid, Pageable page);

  Optional<CreditLedgerRow> findByUserIdAndIdempotencyKey(UUID uid, String key);
}
```

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Append-only ledger (event sourcing); balance = projection
- `balance_after` snapshot for fast read (denormalised; maintained in same tx)
- Unique index on `(user_id, idempotency_key)` — the concurrency primitive
- `CHECK (balance >= 0)` at the DB level — defence in depth against going negative
- `processed_webhook_events` for Stripe idempotency
- Window-function rebuild of the balance from the ledger

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. Why store `balance_after` on every ledger row? Isn't that redundant with `SUM(delta)`?
2. The ledger will grow forever. How do you archive?
3. How do you handle an admin manual adjustment (`ADJUSTMENT`) — is it just another row?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. `SUM(delta)` over a user with 100k ledger rows is an O(n) scan per balance read. `balance_after` is an O(1) read (`SELECT balance FROM credit_balance`). The redundancy is cheap (4 bytes/row) and the two are kept consistent by writing both in the same transaction. If they ever diverge (bug), the ledger is the truth and we rebuild the balance from the ledger.
2. We never delete from the ledger. We partition by `created_at` month (PostgreSQL native partitioning), and after 24 months we move old partitions to cold storage (S3 via `pg_dump` of the partition) and detach them. The `credit_balance` table stays small (one row per active user). Old users who churn keep a zero-balance row; we re-balance quarterly. Regulatory/financial records require 7-year retention, so the cold storage is the compliance copy.
3. Yes — an admin adjustment is a `CreditLedgerRow` with `reason=ADJUSTMENT`, `created_by=adminId`, and a `ref_id` pointing to a `credit_adjustment` row that stores the reason text ("billing error, customer ticket #1234"). The unique index uses the admin-supplied idempotency key (or a generated `{adminId}-{timestamp}`). Every credit change, manual or automated, is one ledger row — there is no other path to mutate the balance. This is the whole point of the design.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- An `UPDATE credit_balance SET balance = balance - 50` without a ledger row — you've lost the audit trail and can't explain why the balance changed.
- Storing only the ledger and computing `SUM(delta)` on every read — works at 1k rows, dies at 100k.
- No `CHECK (balance >= 0)` — a bug can silently make balances negative, and you discover it when a user "generates outreach" for -50 credits.

### Q-Bonus-5: Design the multi-tenant user/org/membership/role schema with Hibernate filters for row-level tenant isolation. Show the schema and the `@Filter` wiring.
- **Difficulty:** Hard
- **Category:** Hibernate/JPA / Database Design / Multi-tenancy
- **Tags:** multi-tenancy, hibernate-filter, row-level-security, tenant_id

**ANSWER:**
AcquisitionOS is a multi-tenant B2B SaaS — every tenant is an `Organisation`, every user belongs to one or more orgs via a `Membership`, and every tenant-scoped table (`leads`, `deals`, `pipelines`, `messages`) carries an `org_id` column. Row-level isolation is enforced at two layers: (1) a **Hibernate `@Filter`** automatically appends `AND org_id = :current_org_id` to every query on tenant-scoped entities, enabled per-request by a filter registry in the `TenantContext` (a `ThreadLocal` set by a servlet filter from the JWT claim); (2) a **PostgreSQL Row-Level Security policy** as a backstop — even if a bug in the Hibernate filter lets a query slip through, the DB itself rejects rows from the wrong tenant. Defence in depth.

**Schema:**
```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email           VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  name            VARCHAR(120),
  password_hash   VARCHAR(120),                    -- NULL for OTP/magic-link-only users
  status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE organisation (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name            VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
  plan            VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'FREE',
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE membership (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id         UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  org_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organisation(id),
  role            VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,            -- OWNER, ADMIN, MEMBER, VIEWER
  status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (user_id, org_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_membership_org ON membership (org_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_membership_user ON membership (user_id);

-- Tenant-scoped table (every tenant table follows this pattern)
CREATE TABLE leads (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id          UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES organisation(id),
  owner_user_id   UUID REFERENCES users(id),       -- assigned rep; nullable for unassigned
  email           VARCHAR(255),
  phone           VARCHAR(40),
  company         VARCHAR(200),
  status          VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW',
  quality_score   INTEGER,
  data            JSONB,                           -- flexible attributes
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_leads_org_owner ON leads (org_id, owner_user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_leads_org_status ON leads (org_id, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_leads_org_score ON leads (org_id, quality_score DESC);

-- Postgres RLS backstop
ALTER TABLE leads ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON leads
  USING (org_id = current_setting('app.current_org_id', true)::uuid);
```

**Hibernate `@Filter` wiring:**
```java
@Entity @Table(name = "leads")
@Filter(name = "tenantFilter", condition = "org_id = :orgId", deduceJoinColumnInsertionOrder = false)
public class Lead {
  @Id private UUID id;
  @Column(name = "org_id") private UUID orgId;
  private UUID ownerUserId;
  private String email, phone, company, status;
  private Integer qualityScore;
  @Column(columnDefinition = "jsonb") private String data;
  @CreatedDate private Instant createdAt;
}

// Enabled per request by a filter that reads the JWT org claim:
@Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TenantFilter implements WebFilter {
  private final EntityManager em;
  public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange ex, WebFilterChain chain) {
    return AuthContext.current().doOnNext(ctx -> {
      if (ctx.isAuthenticated()) {
        em.unwrap(Session.class).enableFilter("tenantFilter")
          .setParameter("orgId", ctx.getOrgId());
      }
    }).then(chain.filter(ex));
  }
}
```

Now every `leadRepository.findAll()` automatically becomes `SELECT ... FROM leads WHERE org_id = ?` — a developer cannot accidentally write a cross-tenant query unless they disable the filter (which is audited).

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- `org_id` on every tenant-scoped table; `membership` as the join with role
- Hibernate `@Filter` enabled per-request from JWT claim via `ThreadLocal`/context
- PostgreSQL RLS as a backstop (`current_setting('app.current_org_id')`)
- Defence in depth: app-layer filter + DB-layer policy
- Composite indexes starting with `org_id` (most selective first for tenant queries)

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. A super-admin needs to read across all tenants for the admin dashboard. How do you bypass the filter safely?
2. What if a user belongs to two orgs and switches context?
3. The Hibernate filter doesn't apply to native SQL queries. How do you protect those?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. The `TenantFilter` checks the user's role; for `SUPER_ADMIN` it does NOT enable the tenant filter, so queries are unscoped. The admin dashboard's repository methods are additionally annotated `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('SUPER_ADMIN')")` so even if a non-admin somehow reached the method, Spring Security blocks it. The RLS policy has a `BYPASSRLS` role for super-admin connections (separate DB user) — so even native SQL is unscoped only for that connection.
2. The JWT carries the `active_org_id` claim (set at login or on `POST /auth/switch-org`). Switching org re-issues the JWT. The `TenantFilter` reads `active_org_id`, not a fixed org — so the user's queries are scoped to whichever org they've currently selected. The `membership` table enforces they can only switch to an org they're a member of.
3. Native queries bypass the Hibernate filter. We forbid raw native SQL in tenant-scoped repositories (code review gate). Where native SQL is unavoidable (e.g., a complex analytics CTE), the developer MUST add `AND org_id = :orgId` explicitly and the PR review checks it. The RLS policy is the backstop — if a developer forgets, the DB still filters. We also have an integration test that creates two tenants' data and asserts every repository returns only the caller's tenant — runs on every PR.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- "We filter by `userId` in the service layer" — one forgotten `if` and you've leaked another tenant's data (this is exactly the bug the pentest found).
- No RLS backstop — the app filter is your only line of defence; a single bypass is a full data breach.
- Indexes not starting with `org_id` — the planner scans the whole table and filters, killing performance at scale.

### Q-Bonus-6: Draw the end-to-end request flow for `POST /api/leads` (create lead), annotating every cross-cutting concern (security, validation, tx, audit, rate-limit, tracing) that fires.
- **Difficulty:** Medium
- **Category:** System Design / Spring Boot AOP
- **Tags:** request-lifecycle, aop, tracing, cross-cutting

**ANSWER:**
This is the "trace one request through the whole stack" question. The candidate should be able to name, in order, every component that touches the request and what it does. Below is the annotated flow for creating a lead, which is representative of every mutating endpoint in AcquisitionOS.

**Flow diagram:**
```
 Client (React SPA, TanStack Query)
   │ POST /api/leads  {email, company, ...}   Idempotency-Key: uuid   Authorization: Bearer aq_live_...
   ▼
 [1] AWS ALB — TLS terminate, WAF rules (SQLi/XSS body scan), forward to ECS task
   │
   ▼
 [2] Tomcat connector — accept, hand to worker thread (Hikari-no, the servlet threadpool)
   │
   ▼
 [3] Spring Security FilterChain (order matters!)
     ├─ SecurityContextHolderFilter        — load SecurityContext from JWT
     ├─ JwtAuthenticationFilter            — verify HS256 with JWT_SECRET, set auth principal
     ├─ ApiKeyAuthFilter (fallback)        — if Bearer starts aq_live_, verify API key hash+scope
     ├─ TenantFilter                       — enable Hibernate tenantFilter with orgId from JWT
     ├─ RateLimitAspect @Around            — Redis sliding-window check; 429 if exceeded
     ├─ CsrfFilter                         — for cookie-auth state-changing methods (checks X-Requested-With or token)
     ├─ RequestLoggingAspect @Around       — start MDC traceId, log method+path
     └─ ExceptionTranslationFilter         — convert AuthenticationException → 401, AccessDenied → 403
   │
   ▼
 [4] DispatcherServlet — route to LeadController.create()
   │
   ▼
 [5] LeadController.create(@Valid @RequestBody LeadCreateRequest, ...)
     ├─ @Valid → BeanValidation (Hibernate Validator) → 400 if email invalid
     ├─ MapStruct: LeadCreateRequest → Lead entity
     └─ calls leadService.create(lead)
   │
   ▼
 [6] LeadService.create()  @Transactional(isolation = READ_COMMITTED)
     ├─ TransactionInterceptor (Spring AOP) — BEGIN; set Hibernate tenantFilter already active
     ├─ AuditAspect @Before — publish "lead.create.initiated" to audit log (async)
     ├─ enrichIfMissing() — call enrichment service (cached, Redis-aside)
     ├─ leadRepository.save(lead)   → Hibernate INSERT into leads (tenantFilter adds org_id=)
     ├─ auditPublisher.publish(new LeadCreated(lead))  — in-process Spring event; @EventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)
     └─ TransactionInterceptor — COMMIT (or rollback on exception → 500)
   │
   ▼
 [7] LeadController returns 201 Created + Location: /api/leads/{id}
   │
   ▼
 [8] ResponseLoggingAspect @Around — log status + duration; MDC cleared
   │
   ▼
 [9] Sentry/OTel — span closed; trace exported to Tempo; metrics incremented (lead_created_total{org})
   │
   ▼
 Client receives 201; TanStack Query invalidates ['leads'] → refetch list.
```

**The AOP aspects in order of execution** (cutpoints on the service/controller):
1. `@RateLimit` (around, controller method) — fastest fail if rate-limited
2. `@AuditLog` (around, service method) — records who did what, async to audit table
3. `@Transactional` (around, service method) — opens the DB transaction
4. `@TenantFiltered` (handled by the per-request `TenantFilter`, not an aspect) — Hibernate filter enabled
5. `@PublishEvent` (after-commit, via `ApplicationEventPublisher`) — fires `LeadCreated` for downstream (pipeline auto-stage, notification, analytics)

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- FilterChain order (security filters beforeDispatcherServlet)
- `@Valid` + Bean Validation (Hibernate Validator) at the controller
- `@Transactional` + `TransactionInterceptor` (Spring AOP) at the service
- Spring `ApplicationEventPublisher` + `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` for in-process decoupling
- MDC trace propagation; OTel span per layer; metrics via Micrometer
- Idempotency-Key + Api-Key fallback paths

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. The audit log is async — what if the audit write fails?
2. Why `AFTER_COMMIT` for the event listener and not just `@EventListener`?
3. Where would you add a circuit breaker on this flow?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. The audit aspect writes to an in-memory bounded queue (Disruptor, 10k capacity); a background drainer flushes to the `audit_log` table in batches of 100. If the queue fills (DB slow), the aspect drops the audit event and increments a `audit_dropped_total` counter — we never block the user request on audit. The audit table itself is partitioned by day; we tolerate losing the last few seconds of audit (the access log + OTel traces are a secondary record). For *security-critical* audits (failed login, role change), we write synchronously and fail the request if the audit write fails — those can't be lost.
2. `@EventListener` fires immediately, inside the transaction; if the listener throws, the transaction rolls back. `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` fires only after the commit succeeds, so a listener failure doesn't undo the business write. This is critical for things like "send a welcome email when a user signs up" — you don't want the email-send to be able to roll back the signup.
3. The `enrichIfMissing` call inside the service hits an external enrichment API. We wrap it in a Resilience4j circuit breaker (`@CircuitBreaker(name="enrichment")`) — if the enrichment provider is down, we save the lead un-enriched (quality_score=null) and queue a background job to enrich later, rather than failing the create. The user gets a 201 with a partially-populated lead; the enrichment completes asynchronously.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- Not knowing the filter chain order — "I think security runs first, then the controller" is too vague for a senior.
- Putting `@Transactional` on the controller — the transaction then spans serialisation/JSON, holding the DB connection for the whole HTTP response.
- Synchronous audit + synchronous email in the same tx as the business write — a slow SMTP server now rolls back your lead create.

### Q-Bonus-7: Draw the zero-downtime deployment flow (blue/green with a DB schema migration). Where can it go wrong and how do you guard each step?
- **Difficulty:** Hard
- **Category:** DevOps / Deployment
- **Tags:** blue-green, flyway, zero-downtime, expand-contract, rollback

**ANSWER:**
Zero-downtime with a schema change is the trickiest deployment scenario because the new code and the new schema must coexist with the old code during the switch. The pattern is **expand–contract**: (1) deploy a schema that is backward-compatible with the old code (the "expand" — add nullable columns, new tables, new indexes `CONCURRENTLY`), (2) deploy the new code (which writes to both old and new), (3) after a soak period, run a "contract" migration (drop old columns) once the old code is fully drained. For a non-expand/contract change (e.g., renaming a column), we do it across two releases: release N renames + writes both, release N+1 drops the old.

**Deployment flow:**
```
 [GREEN = v1.4 live, 4 tasks serving 100% traffic]   [BLUE = v1.5 being deployed]
   │                                                  │
   │  1. Build v1.5 image (GitHub Actions: test → Docker → ECR)
   │  2. Flyway "expand" migration V1.5__expand.sql applied to RDS:
   │     - ALTER TABLE leads ADD COLUMN linkedin_url TEXT;          (nullable — old code ignores)
   │     - CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_leads_org_phone ON leads(org_id, phone);
   │     These run on the live GREEN DB; old code is unaffected.
   │  3. Provision BLUE: 4 ECS Fargate tasks running v1.5, registered to a "blue" target group, 0% traffic.
   │  4. Health check: ALB pings BLUE /actuator/health for 60s; all 4 must be UP.
   │  5. Shift 10% → BLUE (ALB weighted target groups). Watch p95 latency, 5xx, error budget for 10 min.
   │  6. Shift 50% → BLUE. Watch 10 min.
   │  7. Shift 100% → BLUE. GREEN drains: existing requests finish, no new ones; tasks stop after 5 min.
   │  8. GREEN target group deleted. v1.5 is now live.
   │  9. After 24h soak: Flyway "contract" migration V1.5_1__contract.sql:
   │     - DROP COLUMN legacy_phone;   (only safe once no code references it — verify via grep + a canary)
   │ 10. Tag the release; update runbook.
   │
   ▼ Rollback plan: if 5xx > 1% in step 5/6, shift ALB weight back to 100% GREEN (1 command, <30s).
                    Code rollback = instant (just traffic). Schema rollback = the expand migration
                    is forward-only safe (additive); only the contract step is irreversible, and
                    we run it 24h later after confidence.
```

**Where it goes wrong + guard:**
| Step | Failure | Guard |
|---|---|---|
| 2 (expand migration) | `CREATE INDEX` locks the table for writes | Use `CONCURRENTLY` (no write lock, longer runtime); monitor pg_stat_progress |
| 3 (BLUE provision) | New code can't connect to RDS (security group) | `actuator/health/db` reports DOWN; ALB keeps BLUE at 0%; alert fires |
| 4 (health check) | App starts but a cache warmup is missing → first requests slow | Add `/actuator/health/readiness` that returns UP only after cache warmup completes |
| 5 (10% shift) | v1.5 has a bug that 10% of users hit | Automated rollback on 5xx > 1% (CloudWatch alarm → Lambda → ALB weight reset) |
| 6 (50%) | Schema contract accidentally applied early | Contract migration is a *separate* deploy, 24h later, with a manual gate |
| 7 (drain GREEN) | Long-polling requests on GREEN hang | Connection-draining timeout 300s; after that the ALB closes them |
| 9 (contract) | Old column still referenced by a missed code path | `grep` + a canary release of the contract; if any 500s, restore from snapshot (RDS PITR) |

**KEY TERMS TO MENTION:**
- Expand–contract (a.k.a. parallel-change) — additive first, destructive later
- `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (no write lock)
- Flyway versioned + repeatable migrations; out-of-order detection OFF in prod
- ALB weighted target groups for gradual traffic shift
- `/actuator/health` vs `/actuator/health/readiness` (liveness vs readiness)
- Automated rollback on SLO breach (CloudWatch alarm → Lambda)
- RDS point-in-time recovery for the "contract went wrong" case

**FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS:**
1. The contract step drops a column. How do you know no code references it?
2. What if the expand migration itself fails halfway (3 of 5 statements ran)?
3. How do you handle a migration that adds a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table?

**FOLLOW-UP ANSWERS:**
1. Code review + `grep -r legacy_phone src/` returns nothing; a canary deploy of the contract to one task first (via a feature flag that runs the contract only when `contract.enabled=true`); watch that task's 5xx for an hour. We also keep the column for one more release — we only drop in release N+2 after release N+1 has run for a week with no references. Belt and suspenders.
2. Flyway wraps each migration file in a transaction (Postgres DDL is transactional) — a halfway failure rolls back the whole file, and Flyway marks it `failed` in `flyway_schema_history`. The fix: correct the script, `flyway repair` (clears the failed row), redeploy. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` is the one DDL that *isn't* transactional and can leave a partial index — we `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and retry.
3. Three-step: (1) `ALTER TABLE leads ADD COLUMN score INTEGER;` (nullable, instant on PG 11+ — no rewrite); (2) backfill in batches of 10k with `UPDATE leads SET score = ... WHERE id BETWEEN ... AND score IS NULL;` throttled to avoid replica lag; (3) once all rows have a value, `ALTER TABLE leads ALTER COLUMN score SET NOT NULL;` (fast — PG verifies the constraint on existing rows). Never `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN score INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;` on PG < 11 — it rewrites the whole table, locking it.

**RED FLAGS TO AVOID:**
- "We just run the migration in the deploy step" without separating expand and contract — a non-additive change blocks zero-downtime.
- `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` on a large table — write lock for minutes.
- No automated rollback — relying on a human to notice 5xx and run a command at 3am.

### Q-Bonus-8: A Spring Batch job scraping 50k leads crashes at row 30,012. How do you design it so a restart resumes from row 30,012 and doesn't re-scrape the first 30k?
- **Difficulty:** Hard
- **Category:** Spring Batch / Background Jobs
- **Tags:** spring-batch, checkpoint, restartable, chunk-oriented

**ANSWER:**
Spring Batch's chunk-oriented step model gives us this for free if we use it correctly: the `JobRepository` persists the step's `ExecutionContext` after every chunk commit, so a restart re-reads the last committed position. The key is to use a `JdbcPagingItemReader` (or a `RepositoryItemReader` with paging) rather than a cursor-based reader — cursors don't survive a JVM restart because the DB result-set is gone. The reader's page index is stored in the step's `ExecutionContext` (`reader.page`), and on restart the reader re-issues the query starting at that page.

**Config:**
```java
@Bean
public Job leadDiscoveryJob(Step scrapeStep) {
  return jobs.get("leadDiscoveryJob")
      .incrementer(new RunIdIncrementer())   // new params each run; restart uses the same params
      .start(scrapeStep)
      .build();
}

@Bean
public Step scrapeStep(ItemReader<RawLead> reader, ItemProcessor<RawLead, Lead> processor,
                      ItemWriter<Lead> writer, PlatformTransactionManager tx) {
  return steps.get("scrapeStep")
      .<RawLead, Lead>chunk(200)             // commit every 200 rows → checkpoint
      .reader(reader)
      .processor(processor)
      .writer(writer)
      .transactionManager(tx)
      .faultTolerant()
        .retryLimit(3)
        .retry(TransientNetworkException.class)   // retry transient HTTP failures
      .skipLimit(50)
      .skip(MalformedLeadException.class)          // skip garbage, don't fail the job
      .listener(new ChunkProgressListener())      // logs chunk progress
      .build();
}

@Bean
@StepScope
public JdbcPagingItemReader<RawLead> leadReader(@Value("#{jobParameters['since']}") LocalDate since) {
  return new JdbcPagingItemReaderBuilder<RawLead>()
      .name("leadReader")
      .dataSource(dataSource)
      .selectClause("SELECT id, source_url, raw_json")
      .fromClause("FROM raw_lead_queue")
```
